Keep the old endpoint up and watch its logs during migration

subjective.question: Case study: a multiplayer game has three parts. Real-time match traffic uses UDP, and ISP partners need fixed IPs. A matchmaking REST API needs path-based routing. A web store serves mostly static content. Players are in India, Europe and the US. Design the edge on AWS, and name the GCP and Azure equivalents.
subjective.answer: I would split traffic by protocol. On AWS, match traffic goes to a Network Load Balancer with UDP listeners in each game region. In front of it I would put AWS Global Accelerator. It gives two static anycast IPs for partners to allow-list, and it carries packets over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location. The matchmaking API runs behind an Application Load Balancer, which provides Layer 7 path routing, TLS termination and AWS WAF. The store goes on CloudFront with an S3 or ALB origin, so static files are served close to players. On GCP I would use an external passthrough Network Load Balancer for UDP, a global external Application Load Balancer for the API, and Cloud CDN for the store. On Azure I would use Azure Load Balancer for UDP, and Azure Front Door or Application Gateway for HTTPS and caching. The main trade-off is that Layer 4 balancers give low latency and UDP support but cannot do content-based routing.
keyPoints: Layer 4 (NLB) for UDP game traffic, Layer 7 (ALB) for the HTTP API
Global Accelerator for static anycast IPs and backbone routing
CDN for the static store
GCP: passthrough NLB, global external ALB, Cloud CDN; Azure: Load Balancer, Front Door or Application Gateway
Explain the trade-off between Layer 4 speed and Layer 7 features

subjective.question: Put in order the steps to move a production domain's DNS to a new DNS provider without downtime, and explain why the order matters.
subjective.answer: Step 1: export every record from the old provider: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT (SPF, DKIM, verification) and CAA. Step 2: create a matching zone at the new provider. Step 3: test the new zone by querying the new name servers directly, for example dig @new-ns www.example.com. Check that every record matches. Step 4: a day or more ahead, lower the TTL on the NS records and key records at the old provider. Step 5: change the name servers at the registrar. Step 6: keep the old zone running and unchanged. The parent zone's NS delegation can be cached for up to two days, so some resolvers will still query the old provider. Step 7: watch traffic, email delivery and certificate renewals. Step 8: decommission the old zone only after the old TTLs have passed. The order matters because resolvers can hit either provider during the switch. Both must give the same answers, or users see random failures. If DNSSEC is enabled, handle the DS record carefully, or validation will fail.
keyPoints: Export and copy every record, including MX, TXT and CAA
Test the new name servers directly before switching
Lower TTLs well in advance
Change NS at the registrar and keep both zones identical while caches expire
Handle DNSSEC DS records; decommission the old zone last

subjective.question: A frontend team wants to turn on HTTP/2 Server Push to speed up first page load. What do you advise, and what would you use instead?
subjective.answer: I would advise against it. Chrome removed Server Push support in 2022, and most browsers and CDNs no longer rely on it. HTTP/3 deployments rarely support it either. Even when it worked, it often wasted bandwidth. The server could not tell what the browser already had in cache, so it pushed CSS and JavaScript the client did not need. That competed with resources the page did need. Better options give the same early start without those problems. First, use 103 Early Hints with Link: rel=preload headers. While the server is still building the HTML, the browser can start fetching critical assets, and it respects its own cache. Second, use preload and preconnect hints in the HTML. Third, serve assets from a CDN close to users, with long cache lifetimes and content-hashed file names. Finally, measure with real user monitoring, because the real bottleneck is often render-blocking JavaScript.
keyPoints: Major browsers such as Chrome removed Server Push; it is effectively dead
Push ignored the client cache and wasted bandwidth
Use 103 Early Hints and rel=preload or preconnect
Use a CDN with long-lived, hashed assets
Measure with real user monitoring before optimising

subjective.question: After a certificate renewal, desktop browsers load https://api.example.com fine. The Android app, curl and a Java client fail with certificate errors. Read the output below, then explain the cause and fix.

code.code:
$ openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com
Certificate chain
 0 s:CN = api.example.com
   i:C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11
---
Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

subjective.answer: The chain shows only one certificate, the leaf. The server is not sending the intermediate certificate (R11) that links the leaf to a trusted root. Desktop browsers often hide this problem. They may already have the intermediate cached, or they fetch it using the AIA URL inside the certificate. Android apps, curl and Java usually do not, so they cannot build the chain and the handshake fails. The fix is to configure the server or load balancer with the full chain, leaf plus intermediates: for example fullchain.pem in NGINX (ssl_certificate), or the chain field when importing a certificate. Then rerun openssl s_client. It should show two certificates in the chain and 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)'. To prevent this, make chain verification part of the renewal automation, and monitor the endpoint with a non-browser client, not only a browser.
keyPoints: Only the leaf is sent; the intermediate is missing
Browsers hide it through caching or AIA fetching; other clients fail
Serve the full chain, e.g. fullchain.pem
Verify with openssl s_client: return code 0
Check the chain with non-browser clients after each renewal

subjective.question: Live cricket scores must reach 5 million concurrent users, with updates every few seconds. Compare short polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets, and pick an approach.
subjective.answer: Naive short polling every 5 seconds from 5 million users is 1 million requests per second. That is too much if each request reaches origin servers. Long polling cuts empty responses, but each client still reconnects after every update, so connection churn stays high. Server-Sent Events keep one long-lived HTTP response open for one-way server-to-client updates. They reconnect automatically and work well over HTTP/2, which suits a score feed. WebSockets are full duplex. They are useful for chat or betting but add complexity in proxies and fan-out, and scores do not need client-to-server messages. Because every user sees the same score, I would start with short polling of a small JSON file cached at the CDN with a 2–3 second TTL. The CDN absorbs the 1 million QPS, and the origin sees only a few requests per second for each edge location. If the product needs sub-second updates, I would move to SSE through a dedicated fan-out tier.
keyPoints: Estimate it: 5 million users ÷ 5 s = 1 million QPS
Long polling still churns connections
SSE fits one-way feeds; WebSockets fit two-way messaging
Identical data for all users makes CDN-cached polling very cheap
Choose by the latency requirement and the cost of fan-out

subjective.question: Estimate write QPS, read QPS and 5-year storage for a URL shortener. It creates 100 million new short URLs per month, with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. State your assumptions.
subjective.answer: Assumptions: a month is about 2.6 million seconds, peak traffic is 3 times average, each record is about 500 bytes (short code, long URL, owner, timestamps), and records are kept for 5 years. Average write QPS is 100 million ÷ 2.6 million ≈ 40, so peak is about 120. Reads are 100 times writes, so about 4,000 QPS average and about 12,000 QPS at peak. Total records over 5 years are 100 million × 60 = 6 billion. Storage is 6 billion × 500 bytes = 3 TB, or about 9 TB with 3 replicas. That is modest and fits a sharded key-value store. The design follows from these numbers. Writes are easy. Reads dominate, so a cache in front of the store matters most, because popular links take a large share of traffic. A short code of 7 characters from 62 symbols gives about 3.5 trillion combinations, far more than 6 billion.
keyPoints: State the month length, peak factor, record size and retention
Writes are about 40/s average (about 120 at peak); reads about 4,000/s (about 12,000 at peak)
5-year storage is about 3 TB raw, about 9 TB with replicas
The workload is read-heavy, so caching is the key design point
Check the key space: 62^7 is much larger than 6 billion

subjective.question: This client wrapper is used for POST /payments. It caused duplicate charges and made an outage worse. Find the mistakes and fix them.
subjective.answer: It retries every non-2xx response, including 400, 401, 403 and 404. Those will never succeed, so retrying only adds load. Retry only network errors, 429, 502, 503 and 504. It retries a non-idempotent POST. If a 504 happens after the server has already charged the card, the retry charges again. Send an Idempotency-Key header so the server can safely detect duplicates. There is no backoff or jitter, so thousands of clients retry at the same moment and keep the backend down. That is a retry storm. Use exponential backoff with jitter, and honour any Retry-After header on 429 or 503. Ten attempts is too many; limit it to about 3 and set an overall deadline. There is no request timeout, so a hung connection blocks forever. Use an AbortController timeout. Network errors throw out of the loop without any retry, so wrap the fetch in try/catch. Add a circuit breaker so the client stops calling a service that keeps failing.
keyPoints: Do not retry 4xx errors except 429
Make POST retries safe with an idempotency key
Use exponential backoff with jitter and honour Retry-After
Cap the attempts and add per-request timeouts
Handle network exceptions and add a circuit breaker

subjective.question: Photo uploads above 1 MB fail with HTTP 413 at an NGINX reverse proxy. After that is fixed, 20 MB uploads from slow mobile networks fail with 504 or timeouts. Explain both failures and propose a better design.
subjective.answer: 413 means Payload Too Large. NGINX's default client_max_body_size is 1 MB, so bigger bodies are rejected before they reach the app. Setting it to, say, 25 MB fixes that. The second failure comes from timeouts. On a slow 3G link a 20 MB upload can take minutes. Directives such as client_body_timeout, proxy_read_timeout and proxy_send_timeout default to 60 seconds, and a load balancer idle timeout or app server timeout can also cut the request. Raising every timeout is fragile and ties up proxy and app resources. A better design takes uploads off the app servers. The API returns a pre-signed URL for S3, Cloud Storage or Azure Blob, and the client uploads directly to the object store. Use multipart or resumable uploads so a dropped connection resumes instead of restarting. Compress or resize images on the device first. An event from the object store then triggers thumbnail processing.
keyPoints: 413 comes from the default 1 MB client_max_body_size
Timeouts are client_body_timeout, proxy timeouts and the LB idle timeout
Do not just raise every timeout; it wastes proxy resources
Use pre-signed direct-to-object-storage uploads
Use multipart or resumable uploads and client-side compression

subjective.question: Compare three TLS choices for a load-balanced web app: terminating at the load balancer, terminating and re-encrypting to the backend, and TLS passthrough. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: Terminating at the load balancer means the balancer decrypts and sends plain HTTP to the backends. It is simple and cheap, and it enables Layer 7 features such as path routing, WAF, header changes and cookies. Certificates sit in one place, such as ACM. The risk is unencrypted traffic inside the network, which many compliance rules do not allow. Re-encryption terminates at the balancer and opens a new TLS connection to the backend. You keep all Layer 7 features and get encryption in transit end to end. The cost is certificates on the backends and a little more CPU. This is my default for regulated workloads. Passthrough uses a Layer 4 balancer, such as an NLB TCP listener, that forwards the encrypted stream untouched. The backend holds the keys and can read client certificates directly, which suits strict key custody or custom protocols. You lose Layer 7 routing and WAF, and you need Proxy Protocol or a similar method to see the client IP.
keyPoints: Termination at the LB is simple, enables Layer 7 features, but is plaintext inside
Re-encryption gives end-to-end encryption and keeps Layer 7 features
Passthrough uses Layer 4; the backend holds the keys
Passthrough loses WAF and content routing
Choose based on compliance and key-custody needs

subjective.question: Case study: an Indian payments startup needs an API that keeps data in India and authenticates partners with mutual TLS. Partners allow-list fixed IPs, and the service must survive a regional outage within minutes. Design the request path on AWS.
subjective.answer: I would run active-passive in two Indian regions, Mumbai (ap-south-1) and Hyderabad (ap-south-2), so data stays in India. Each region has an Application Load Balancer with mutual TLS in verify mode against a trust store of partner CAs. If partners require the backend itself to check certificates, I would use an NLB with TCP passthrough instead. For fixed IPs and fast failover, I would place Global Accelerator in front, with an endpoint group in each region and health checks. Partners allow-list two static anycast IPs, and failover does not wait for DNS caches. If I used Route 53 failover records instead, I would set a 60-second TTL with health checks and accept that some clients cache longer. Data replicates to Hyderabad, with the recovery point objective agreed with the business. Every payment request carries an idempotency key, because failover and timeouts cause retries, and double charges are unacceptable. Clients get clear status codes: 401 or 403 for authentication, 429 for rate limits, 503 with Retry-After during failover.
keyPoints: Two Indian regions for data residency and disaster recovery
Mutual TLS at the ALB, or NLB passthrough if the backend must verify certificates
Static IPs and fast failover through Global Accelerator, versus DNS TTL limits
Idempotency keys make retries during failover safe
Clear status codes and Retry-After for clients

subjective.question: An Indian e-commerce site normally handles 50 million daily users making about 20 requests each. For a flash sale, 5 million users arrive in the first 10 minutes and each makes about 20 requests in that window. Estimate the sale-peak QPS, compare it with normal load, and say how you would prepare.
subjective.answer: Normal average load is 50 million × 20 ÷ 86,400 ≈ 11,600 QPS. Even with a normal peak factor of 3, that is about 35,000 QPS. Sale traffic is 5 million × 20 = 100 million requests in 600 seconds, about 167,000 QPS on average. Traffic is spikier in the first minute, so I would plan for about 300,000 QPS. That is roughly 15 to 25 times a normal day, so a normal peak factor would badly under-provision. To prepare: serve static assets and product pages from a CDN. Cache catalogue and price data in memory, and pre-warm the caches. Pre-scale servers and load balancers ahead of time instead of waiting for autoscaling, which reacts in minutes. Put a virtual waiting room or queue in front of checkout. Protect inventory and payment services with rate limits that return 429 with Retry-After. Load-test at the target QPS beforehand.
keyPoints: Normal: about 11,600 QPS average, about 35,000 at peak
Sale: 100 million requests in 600 s ≈ 167,000 QPS; plan for about 300,000
Event spikes break normal peak factors
CDN, caching and pre-scaling, because autoscaling lags
Waiting room, 429 rate limiting and load testing

steps.overview: This step teaches you to scale the web and app tier by adding identical, stateless servers behind a load balancer, instead of buying ever-bigger machines. You will learn how L4 and L7 load balancers route traffic, where session state must go so any server can handle any request, and how CDNs take load off your origin. These ideas come up constantly in SAA-C03 high-availability questions, in GCP and Azure architect case studies, and in almost every system design interview.
objectives: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling and choose the right one for a given workload and failure requirement
Select an L4 or L7 load balancer and a routing algorithm (round robin, least connections, consistent hashing) for a scenario
Move session state out of web servers into a shared store such as Redis/ElastiCache or DynamoDB, or into signed tokens
Design a multi-AZ web tier with an Auto Scaling group and health checks that survives one availability zone failing
Explain when a CDN can cache static and dynamic content, and how TTLs and cache keys affect hit ratio

concepts.explanation: Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine with more CPU and RAM. It is simple but has a hardware ceiling, usually needs a restart, and leaves a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more identical machines behind a load balancer. It gives near-linear capacity and fault tolerance, but only works cleanly if servers are stateless.

A stateless server keeps no client-specific data between requests in its own memory or disk. Any instance can serve any request, so you can add, remove or replace instances freely. State still exists, but it lives in a shared store (cache, database, object storage) or in the client (a signed token).

An L4 load balancer routes by IP address, port and protocol (TCP/UDP) without reading the request content; it is very fast and can preserve client IPs. An L7 load balancer understands HTTP/HTTPS, so it can route by path, host header, headers or query strings, terminate TLS and set cookies. On AWS, Network Load Balancer is L4 and Application Load Balancer is L7; on GCP and Azure the equivalents are the network/passthrough vs application load balancers, and Azure Load Balancer (L4) vs Application Gateway (L7).

Round robin sends each new request to the next server in turn; it is fair only when requests cost about the same. Least connections (on AWS ALB: least outstanding requests) sends the request to the server with the fewest active requests, which handles uneven or long-running requests better. Weighted variants let bigger servers take more traffic.

Servers and keys are placed on a hash ring, and each key goes to the next server clockwise. When a server is added or removed, only about 1/N of keys move, unlike simple modulo hashing where most keys remap. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out uneven load. It is used when a key should keep hitting the same node, for example cache shards, not for general stateless web traffic.

The load balancer pins a user to one server, usually with a cookie, so in-memory session data stays usable. This hurts scaling: load becomes uneven, new instances get little traffic, scale-in or a crash logs users out, and one AZ failure loses all sessions held there. The replacement is externalised state: a shared session store or stateless signed tokens such as JWTs.

Session data is written to a fast shared store keyed by session ID, usually Redis (Amazon ElastiCache, Memorystore, Azure Cache for Redis) or a key-value database like DynamoDB with TTL. Every web server reads the same data, so any instance can serve the user. Make the store itself highly available, for example Redis with replicas across AZs, or it becomes the new single point of failure.

Instances run in an Auto Scaling group spread across at least two (ideally three) availability zones behind a regional load balancer. Health checks remove failed instances, and Auto Scaling replaces them. You must keep enough spare capacity in the remaining AZs to carry peak load when one AZ goes down.

A CDN such as Amazon CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door or Cloudflare caches content at edge locations close to users. Static assets (images, JS, CSS, often stored in S3) cache with long TTLs and versioned file names. Dynamic content can still benefit: short TTLs (even a few seconds) for popular pages, careful cache keys, and TLS termination plus persistent connections to the origin.

The cache key decides which requests share a cached object; adding unnecessary headers, cookies or query strings to it fragments the cache and lowers the hit ratio. The TTL decides how long an object stays at the edge before revalidation. Use origin Cache-Control headers to control TTL, and invalidation or versioned URLs to push changes.

keyFacts: Horizontal scaling needs stateless servers; vertical scaling is a quick fix but keeps a single point of failure and a hardware ceiling.
AWS ALB = Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS, path and host routing, WebSockets, gRPC); NLB = Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS, static IP per AZ, ultra-low latency); Gateway Load Balancer is for third-party network appliances.
ALB routing algorithms: round robin (default), least outstanding requests, and weighted random. NLB uses flow hashing.
Cross-zone load balancing is on by default for ALB and off by default for NLB.
ALB sticky sessions use either a load-balancer cookie (AWSALB, duration-based) or an application cookie; the exam answer for scalable sessions is usually ElastiCache or DynamoDB instead.
ALB deregistration delay (connection draining) defaults to 300 seconds, letting in-flight requests finish before an instance is removed.
Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when one of N nodes changes; modulo hashing remaps most keys.
Survive one AZ loss: with N AZs, each AZ must hold peak/(N-1) capacity. Three AZs need 1.5x peak in total; two AZs need 2x peak.
CloudFront default TTL is 24 hours unless the origin sends Cache-Control headers or you change the cache policy; use versioned file names rather than frequent invalidations.
Use Origin Access Control (OAC) so the S3 bucket behind CloudFront is private and only reachable through the CDN.

example.caption: Worked estimate: a web tier that survives losing one AZ (AWS)
example.code:
Requirement: peak = 6,000 req/s, one instance handles 1,000 req/s
Need at peak: 6 healthy instances, even with one AZ down

Option A - 2 AZs:
  If one AZ fails, the other must carry 6 instances
  Per AZ = 6 -> total = 12 instances (2.0x peak)

Option B - 3 AZs:
  If one AZ fails, the other two must carry 6
  Per AZ = 6 / 2 = 3 -> total = 9 instances (1.5x peak)
  -> 3 AZs is cheaper and still survives one AZ loss

Design:
  Route 53 -> CloudFront (static from private S3 via OAC,
                          dynamic with short TTL)
  -> ALB (subnets in AZ-a, AZ-b, AZ-c, cross-zone on)
  -> Auto Scaling group: min 9, desired 9, max 18,
     ELB health checks, target tracking on CPU or
     requests per target
  -> No sticky sessions; sessions in ElastiCache for Redis
     (primary + replicas in other AZs, Multi-AZ failover)
  -> Database: RDS/Aurora Multi-AZ (covered in later steps)

AZ-b fails:
  ALB health checks mark AZ-b targets unhealthy
  Traffic shifts to AZ-a and AZ-c (3 + 3 = 6 = peak)
  Users stay logged in: sessions are in Redis, not on servers
  ASG launches replacements in healthy AZs

pitfalls: Choosing sticky sessions to 'fix' logouts after scaling out. It hides the real problem; the scalable answer is a shared session store or signed tokens.
Sizing the Auto Scaling group for normal load only. If you lose one AZ out of two, you lose half your capacity at the worst moment unless you pre-provision for it.
Picking NLB when the question needs path-based or host-based routing, or picking ALB when the question needs a static IP, UDP or extreme throughput at low latency.
Moving sessions to a single Redis node in one AZ. You have just moved the single point of failure; use replicas across AZs with automatic failover.
Putting cookies, Authorization headers or all query strings in the CDN cache key by default, which kills the hit ratio, or caching personalised pages publicly and leaking user data.
Using consistent hashing for a general stateless web tier. It creates hot spots and affinity you do not need; round robin or least connections is the usual right choice there.

workflow.title: How a request flows through a scalable, AZ-resilient web tier

steps.label: DNS resolves to the CDN
steps.detail: Route 53 or another DNS returns the CDN edge address closest to the user.

steps.label: Edge serves cached content
steps.detail: The CDN returns static assets and short-TTL dynamic pages from cache, and forwards misses to the origin.

steps.label: Load balancer picks a target
steps.detail: The regional ALB routes by path or host and uses round robin or least outstanding requests across healthy targets in all AZs.

steps.label: Stateless instance handles request
steps.detail: Any instance in the Auto Scaling group can serve the user because it holds no local session data.

steps.label: Session read from shared store
steps.detail: The instance loads the session by ID from Redis or DynamoDB, or validates a signed token.

steps.label: Health checks remove failures
steps.detail: If an instance or a whole AZ fails, health checks stop traffic to it and connection draining finishes in-flight requests.

steps.label: Auto Scaling restores capacity
steps.detail: The group launches replacement instances in healthy AZs and scales out on CPU or request-count targets.

project.title: multi-az-web-tier
project.summary: A stateless Node.js cart API whose session data lives in Redis, not in server memory. Two replicas sit behind an nginx L7 load balancer (least connections) with an edge-style cache, so you can kill one instance and keep your cart. It also includes Terraform that builds the same web tier on AWS to survive one Availability Zone going down: an ALB and Auto Scaling group across AZs, Multi-AZ ElastiCache for sessions, and CloudFront in front. app/server.js shows the stateless service and the external session store. nginx/nginx.conf shows L7 balancing, failover and the cache key. docker-compose.yml runs the local lab. infra/main.tf builds the multi-AZ ALB and Auto Scaling group. infra/session_cdn.tf adds the Multi-AZ session store and the CDN.

files.code:
# multi-az-web-tier (Step 2: Scaling the stateless tier)

## What it shows
- **Horizontal scaling**: two identical app replicas. You add capacity by adding servers, not by buying a bigger one.
- **Stateless service**: the app keeps no user data in memory. The cart lives in Redis under `sess:<sid>`, with a 30-minute TTL.
- **L7 load balancing**: nginx (locally) and an ALB (on AWS) route HTTP requests.
  - nginx uses `least_conn`.
  - The ALB uses `least_outstanding_requests`.
  - Round robin is the default in both.
- **No sticky sessions**: any instance can serve any request.
- **Edge caching**: `/api/products` is public and cacheable.
  - Cache key = scheme + host + path.
  - It returns `X-Cache-Status: MISS`, then `HIT`.
  - `/api/cart/*` is `private, no-store`, so it is never cached.

## Hands-on task: survive one AZ going down
```
Users -> CloudFront (edge cache)
      -> ALB (nodes in AZ-a and AZ-b)
      -> ASG: min 2 EC2, spread over AZ-a / AZ-b
      -> ElastiCache Redis: primary in one AZ, replica in the other, auto-failover
```
If AZ-a fails:
1. ALB health checks (`/healthz`) mark the AZ-a targets unhealthy. Traffic goes to AZ-b.
2. The ASG launches replacement instances in the healthy AZ.
3. ElastiCache promotes the replica. Sessions survive, so users stay logged in.

Local simulation: `docker compose stop app1`. Your next request still shows the same cart, now `servedBy: app2`.

## Checkpoint: why sticky sessions hurt scaling
With stickiness, the balancer pins each user to one server. This causes four problems:
- **Uneven load**: heavy users pile onto some servers.
- **Slow scale-in**: new servers get no old users, and you cannot remove a server without breaking its sessions.
- **Lost sessions**: if a server or AZ dies, its sessions die with it.
- **Weaker hash routing**: consistent hashing on a cookie only reduces reshuffling when servers change. It is still affinity.

The replacement has two parts:
1. Keep the service **stateless**.
2. Put the session in an **external store** (Redis/ElastiCache, DynamoDB) or in a signed token (JWT).

Then the balancer can use plain round robin or least connections.

## Cost warning
The Terraform creates billable resources (ALB, EC2, ElastiCache, CloudFront). Run `terraform destroy` when done.

# Local lab: 2 stateless replicas + Redis session store + nginx L7 load balancer.
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine          # stands in for ElastiCache

  app1: &app
    build:
      context: ./app
      dockerfile_inline: |
        FROM node:22-alpine
        WORKDIR /app
        COPY package.json .
        RUN npm install --omit=dev
        COPY server.js .
        CMD ["node", "server.js"]
    environment:
      PORT: "3000"
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      INSTANCE_ID: app1
    depends_on: [redis]

  app2:
    <<: *app                       # identical image = horizontal scaling
    environment:
      PORT: "3000"
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      INSTANCE_ID: app2

  lb:
    image: nginx:1.27-alpine
    ports:
      - "8080:80"                  # clients only talk to the load balancer
    volumes:
      - ./nginx/nginx.conf:/etc/nginx/nginx.conf:ro
    depends_on: [app1, app2]

revision.examFocus: This step maps to SAA-C03 Domain 2 (Design Resilient Architectures) and Domain 3 (Design High-Performing Architectures). It also maps to the reliability and scalability parts of the Google Professional Cloud Architect case studies and the AZ-305 'Design infrastructure solutions' area. Exams rarely ask for definitions. They describe a symptom, such as users logged out after scale-out, an outage during an AZ failure, a slow global site or a client that needs a fixed IP. You must pick the load balancer, session store, capacity plan or CDN setting that fixes the root cause with the least operational overhead.

compare.difference: ALB reads HTTP, so it can route by path, host or header and can authenticate users. NLB only sees TCP/UDP flows, but it gives a static IP per AZ and very high throughput at low latency.
compare.chooseA: Choose ALB when the question mentions URL paths, hostnames, microservices behind one endpoint, WebSockets, gRPC, WAF or Cognito/OIDC login at the load balancer.
compare.chooseB: Choose NLB when the question mentions UDP, non-HTTP TCP, a static or Elastic IP for firewall allow-listing, millions of requests per second or preserving the client source IP at L4.

compare.b: Externalised session store (ElastiCache / DynamoDB) or signed tokens (JWT)
compare.difference: Stickiness pins a user to one instance, so load becomes uneven and sessions die with that instance. An external store or token lets any instance serve any request.
compare.chooseA: Choose stickiness only as a short-term fix for a legacy app that cannot be changed, and only when losing a session on instance failure is acceptable.
compare.chooseB: Choose an external store or tokens whenever the question says scalable, fault tolerant, Auto Scaling, users must not be logged out, or stateless.

compare.difference: ElastiCache gives sub-millisecond in-memory reads, but you must configure Multi-AZ replicas for durability. DynamoDB is serverless, durable and multi-AZ by default, with TTL to expire old sessions.
compare.chooseA: Choose ElastiCache when the question stresses lowest latency or high request rates and you can run a Multi-AZ replication group with automatic failover.
compare.chooseB: Choose DynamoDB when the question stresses serverless, least operational overhead, durability or automatic expiry using TTL.

compare.difference: Invalidation removes cached objects at the edge after the fact, and it is limited and billed beyond a free monthly allowance. Versioned names create a new cache key, so new content is served instantly with no purge.
compare.chooseA: Choose invalidation for an emergency fix, such as wrong or sensitive content already cached.
compare.chooseB: Choose versioned names for routine deployments of static assets, combined with long TTLs.

compare.a: Azure Front Door / Google global external Application Load Balancer
compare.b: Azure Application Gateway / regional load balancers
compare.difference: Front Door and Google's global L7 load balancer work at the edge across regions, with an anycast entry point, CDN and WAF. Application Gateway is a regional L7 load balancer inside a virtual network.
compare.chooseA: Choose the global option for multi-region users, global failover or edge acceleration.
compare.chooseB: Choose the regional option when all traffic stays in one region and you need L7 routing or WAF in front of VNet backends.

cues.cue: Users are logged out randomly after the Auto Scaling group scales out
cues.pick: Move session state to ElastiCache (Multi-AZ) or DynamoDB
cues.why: The root cause is state held on the instance; stickiness only hides it.

cues.cue: Partner needs to allow-list a fixed IP address
cues.pick: NLB with Elastic IPs, or AWS Global Accelerator in front of an ALB
cues.why: ALB IP addresses change, while NLB and Global Accelerator give stable IPs.

cues.cue: Route /api to one service and /images to another behind one DNS name
cues.pick: ALB with path-based listener rules
cues.why: Path routing needs Layer 7, which NLB cannot see.

cues.cue: Application must keep full capacity if one AZ fails
cues.pick: ASG across 3 AZs sized at peak/(N-1) per AZ, behind an ALB
cues.why: Capacity must be pre-provisioned because scaling after an AZ failure is too slow and may compete for capacity.

cues.cue: Requests vary a lot in processing time and some instances overload
cues.pick: ALB least outstanding requests algorithm
cues.why: It sends new requests to the target with the fewest in-flight requests instead of rotating blindly.

cues.cue: S3 content must only be reachable through the CDN
cues.pick: CloudFront with Origin Access Control and a bucket policy
cues.why: OAC lets only CloudFront sign requests to a private bucket; it replaces the legacy OAI.

cues.cue: Low cache hit ratio on CloudFront
cues.pick: Trim the cache key (cache policy) and forward extra values using an origin request policy
cues.why: Every header, cookie or query string in the cache key splits the cache into more variants.

cues.cue: Distributed cache cluster nodes are added often and most keys miss afterwards
cues.pick: Consistent hashing
cues.why: Modulo hashing remaps almost all keys when the node count changes.

scenario.situation: A retail company runs its web app on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. During a sale the group scaled out and many customers lost their shopping carts and were logged out. Last month an AZ outage also made the site very slow for an hour. The company wants a solution that scales and survives an AZ failure with minimal code changes. What should a solutions architect recommend?
reasoning: Find the root cause: carts and logins live in instance memory, so new or replaced instances do not have them. The app is stateful.
Reject enabling ALB stickiness. It keeps users on one instance but still loses carts when that instance terminates, and it skews load during scale-out.
Reject a larger instance type (vertical scaling). It does not fix lost state, and it keeps a single point of failure.
Reject NLB. Changing the load balancer type does not solve session state, and the app needs L7 features anyway.
Select a Multi-AZ ElastiCache replication group with automatic failover for sessions and carts. Then raise ASG capacity, ideally across three AZs, so the loss of one AZ still leaves peak capacity.
scenario.answer: Externalise session and cart data to ElastiCache with Multi-AZ replicas and automatic failover, and size the ASG across AZs to absorb the loss of one AZ. This makes the instances stateless, so any instance can serve any user and capacity holds during an AZ outage.

memoryAids: ALB = 'Application, Language-aware' (paths, hosts, headers); NLB = 'Network, No-nonsense' (static IP, UDP, speed); GWLB = 'Guards' (firewalls, IDS appliances).
N-1 rule: 'Plan to lose one.' Each AZ carries peak divided by the number of surviving AZs. Two AZs means double, three AZs means one and a half.
Sessions: 'Don't Stick, Share.' Share state in a shared store or a signed token, never on the box.
cheatSheet: A symptom about lost sessions means an external store or tokens. Stickiness is almost never the 'most scalable' answer.
A session store in one AZ is still a single point of failure. The answer must say Multi-AZ, replicas or automatic failover.
Need a static IP but also L7 routing? Put Global Accelerator in front of the ALB, or put an NLB with an ALB as its target.
ALB adds WAF, OIDC/Cognito authentication, host, path and header routing, and weighted target groups for blue/green or canary releases.
NLB cross-zone load balancing is off by default, so uneven target counts per AZ give uneven load unless you enable it.
Use deregistration delay to drain in-flight requests before scale-in or deployment. Shorten it for short requests to speed up deployments.
ALB slow start mode warms new targets gradually. Use it when new instances need cache warm-up.
Use ELB health checks in the ASG, not only EC2 status checks, so instances with a broken app are replaced.
CDN for dynamic content: set TTL to 0 or a short value, still route through the edge for TLS and connection reuse, and never cache personalised responses publicly.
Private paid content on CloudFront: use signed URLs for single files and signed cookies for many files.
Azure mapping: Load Balancer = L4, Application Gateway = regional L7, Front Door = global L7 + CDN, Traffic Manager = DNS-based routing.
GCP mapping: Application Load Balancer = L7, Network Load Balancer = L4, Cloud CDN attaches to the external Application Load Balancer, Memorystore holds sessions.
selfCheck: I can explain in two minutes why sticky sessions hurt scaling and failover, and name two things that replace them.
I can pick ALB, NLB, Gateway Load Balancer or Global Accelerator from a one-line requirement and justify the choice.
I can calculate the per-AZ and total capacity a web tier needs to survive the loss of one AZ, for two or three AZs.
I can draw a Multi-AZ web tier: CloudFront, ALB, ASG across AZs, and a Multi-AZ session store, and point out every single point of failure removed.
I can design a CloudFront cache key and TTL strategy that keeps a high hit ratio without leaking personalised data.
I can say when consistent hashing is the right tool (caches, sharded stores) and when round robin or least connections is better (stateless web tiers).

objective.question: A startup runs its web application on a single large EC2 instance. During a sale, traffic doubles and the team upgrades to a bigger instance type. Which limitation of this approach remains?
options: The instance is still a single point of failure, and instance sizes have a hardware ceiling
Larger instance types cannot be placed in a VPC
Vertical scaling forces the application to become stateless
The application can no longer use an Application Load Balancer
objective.explanation: Vertical scaling is a quick fix, but one server is still a single point of failure, and you eventually reach the largest instance size. The other options are false: vertical scaling places no limits on ALB use, statelessness or VPC placement.

objective.question: A gaming company needs a load balancer for a UDP-based game server fleet. Clients must allow-list a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone, and latency must be as low as possible. Which option meets these needs?
options: Network Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Gateway Load Balancer
Application Load Balancer
objective.explanation: NLB works at Layer 4 and supports TCP, UDP and TLS. It gives a static IP per AZ and very low latency. ALB supports only HTTP/HTTPS, and Gateway Load Balancer is meant for network appliances.

objective.question: An e-commerce site wants requests for /api/* to go to one Auto Scaling group and requests for /images/* to go to another. Requests for admin.example.com must go to a third group. What is the simplest solution?
options: One Application Load Balancer with path-based and host-based listener rules
Three Network Load Balancers behind Route 53 weighted routing
A Gateway Load Balancer with three target groups
One Network Load Balancer with three listeners on different ports
objective.explanation: ALB is a Layer 7 load balancer, so it can read paths and host headers and route on them with listener rules. NLB cannot inspect HTTP paths, and Gateway Load Balancer is for third-party appliances.

objective.question: A security team must send all VPC traffic through a fleet of third-party firewall virtual appliances. The fleet must scale horizontally and stay transparent to the traffic. Which AWS service fits best?
options: Gateway Load Balancer
CloudFront with Origin Access Control
Network Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing
Application Load Balancer with WAF
objective.explanation: Gateway Load Balancer is built to deploy, scale and distribute traffic to third-party network appliances such as firewalls and IDS/IPS. ALB and NLB are not designed for transparent appliance insertion, and CloudFront is a CDN.

objective.question: An ALB fronts a reporting service. Some requests finish in 50 ms and others take 20 seconds. With the default algorithm, some targets become overloaded while others sit idle. What should the architect change?
options: Replace the ALB with an NLB that uses flow hashing
Increase the deregistration delay to 600 seconds
Enable sticky sessions with the AWSALB cookie
Switch the target group's algorithm to least outstanding requests
objective.explanation: Round robin ignores how busy a target is. Least outstanding requests sends each new request to the target with the fewest in-flight requests, which suits uneven request durations. Stickiness and flow hashing do not balance by load, and deregistration delay only affects instance removal.

objective.question: A distributed cache uses consistent hashing across 10 nodes. One node is added, making 11. Roughly what share of keys must move to a different node?
options: About 50%
About 90%
All keys must be rehashed
About 9% (around 1/11)
objective.explanation: Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when membership changes, so only the keys the new node takes over are remapped. Modulo hashing (key mod N) would remap most keys, which is roughly the 90% figure.

objective.question: Users of a web application behind an ALB report that their shopping carts empty when the Auto Scaling group scales in. Sessions are kept in instance memory, and ALB stickiness is enabled. What is the MOST scalable fix?
options: Disable scale-in on the Auto Scaling group
Store session data in Amazon ElastiCache or DynamoDB and make the instances stateless
Replace the ALB with an NLB so client IPs map to the same instance
Increase the AWSALB cookie duration to 7 days
objective.explanation: Externalising session state lets any instance serve any user, so losing an instance loses no sessions. Longer cookies, disabled scale-in or IP affinity all keep the state tied to a single server.

objective.question: A web tier needs 12 instances at peak. It is spread evenly across 3 Availability Zones and must handle peak load with no degradation if any one AZ fails. What is the minimum total number of instances?
objective.explanation: With N AZs, each AZ must hold peak/(N-1) capacity: 12/2 = 6 per AZ, so 18 in total (1.5x peak). 12 would fail on AZ loss, and 24 is the figure for a two-AZ design.

objective.question: A Network Load Balancer is enabled in two AZs. AZ-a has 2 registered targets and AZ-b has 8. The targets in AZ-a are overloaded while those in AZ-b are lightly used. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: Cross-zone load balancing is off by default on NLB; enable it or balance targets across AZs
Deregistration delay is too long; reduce it to 30 seconds
Sticky sessions are on by default on NLB; disable them
NLB uses round robin; change it to least outstanding requests
objective.explanation: Cross-zone load balancing is off by default for NLB, so each AZ's node gets an equal share of traffic and sends it only to its own targets. Enabling cross-zone, or evening out the targets, fixes this. NLB uses flow hashing, not least outstanding requests.

objective.question: A team's API requests all finish in under 2 seconds. During scale-in and rolling deployments, each instance stays in the 'draining' state for 5 minutes, which slows deployments. What should they do?
options: Lower the target group's deregistration delay from the 300-second default to a value slightly above the longest request time
Switch from ALB to NLB, which has no draining
Enable sticky sessions so draining finishes faster
Disable health checks on the target group
objective.explanation: Deregistration delay defaults to 300 seconds so that in-flight requests can finish. With short requests, a lower value keeps draining safe and speeds up deployments. Disabling health checks or adding stickiness does not help, and NLB also has deregistration delay.

objective.question: After every deployment, some users see old CSS served by CloudFront for hours. The team currently runs a full invalidation on every release. What is the recommended long-term approach?
options: Disable caching on the distribution and serve from S3 directly
Invalidate /* every 5 minutes with a scheduled job
Use versioned or hashed file names (for example app.3f9a.css) and reference them from the HTML
Set the default TTL to 0 for all objects
objective.explanation: Versioned file names give each release a new cache key, so assets can carry long TTLs and never go stale. Frequent invalidations are slow and can cost money. TTL 0 or disabling caching removes the benefit of the CDN.

objective.question: A company serves static assets from an S3 bucket through CloudFront. Security requires that the bucket cannot be reached directly from the internet, only through CloudFront. What should the architect do?
options: Put an NLB in front of the S3 bucket
Use signed URLs and keep the bucket public
Configure Origin Access Control (OAC) on the distribution and allow only that distribution in the bucket policy
Enable S3 static website hosting with a public bucket policy
objective.explanation: OAC lets CloudFront sign its requests to S3. The bucket policy then allows only that distribution, so the bucket stays private. Public website hosting and a public bucket both break the requirement, and an NLB cannot front S3 this way.

objective.question: A company runs a web application in two Azure regions. It needs one global entry point that terminates HTTPS at the edge, routes each user to the nearest healthy region, applies a Web Application Firewall, and caches static content close to users. Which service meets all these needs?
options: Azure Application Gateway v2 with WAF in each region
Azure Load Balancer (Standard) with a global tier
Azure Front Door (Standard or Premium)
Azure Traffic Manager with performance routing
objective.explanation: Azure Front Door is a global Layer 7 entry point that terminates TLS at the edge, routes to the closest healthy backend, supports WAF, and caches content. Traffic Manager works only through DNS and does no caching or TLS termination. Application Gateway is regional. Azure Load Balancer works at Layer 4, so it cannot cache content or run a WAF.

objective.question: A company serves a web application from Compute Engine managed instance groups in three Google Cloud regions. Users worldwide must connect to a single static IP address, reach the closest healthy region, and get cached static assets from Google's edge. Which design fits?
options: A global external Application Load Balancer with all three instance groups as backends and Cloud CDN enabled on the backend service
A single regional external Application Load Balancer in the busiest region, with Cloud CDN
An internal Application Load Balancer in each region, connected through VPC peering
A regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer in each region, with Cloud DNS geolocation routing
objective.explanation: The global external Application Load Balancer gives one anycast IP, sends users to the nearest healthy backend, and works with Cloud CDN for edge caching. Regional load balancers with DNS routing need several IPs and add DNS failover delay. Internal load balancers are not reachable from the internet. A single regional load balancer does not give multi-region routing.

objective.question: A CloudFront distribution serves versioned static JavaScript and CSS files (for example app.3f9a.js). The cache hit ratio is below 10% even though the files rarely change. The cache behavior uses the policy below. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: User-Agent, all cookies and all query strings are in the cache key, so nearly every viewer creates a unique cache entry
MinTTL of 0 forces CloudFront to revalidate every request with the origin
Gzip and Brotli in the cache key create too many object variants
The DefaultTTL of one day is too short for static files
objective.explanation: Each value in the cache key splits the cache. User-Agent strings, session or tracking cookies, and query strings vary per user, so almost every request misses. For versioned static assets, the cache key should leave out cookies, query strings and User-Agent. Compression settings add only a few variants, and the TTLs are already reasonable.

objective.question: A team is moving user sessions out of EC2 instance memory. The session store must give sub-millisecond reads, be shared by all instances, and keep sessions if a cache node or an entire Availability Zone fails. Which option meets these requirements?
options: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis OSS (or Valkey) replication group with replicas in other AZs, Multi-AZ and automatic failover enabled
A Multi-Attach EBS volume shared by all web instances
An Amazon EFS file system mounted on every instance, with one file per session
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with several nodes spread across AZs
objective.explanation: A Redis OSS or Valkey replication group with Multi-AZ promotes a replica in another AZ when the primary fails, so sessions survive and reads stay in-memory fast. Memcached does not replicate, so the sessions on a failed node are lost. EFS cannot give sub-millisecond reads for session lookups. EBS Multi-Attach works within one AZ only and does not fit this pattern.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group uses ELB health checks behind an ALB. The /health endpoint runs a query against the RDS database before it returns 200. During a 90-second RDS Multi-AZ failover, every instance in the group was terminated and replaced, which caused a long outage. What is the BEST fix?
options: Switch the ASG health check type from ELB to EC2 and remove the ALB health check
Enable sticky sessions so users stay on instances that are still healthy
Make the ALB and ASG health check a shallow liveness check that does not depend on downstream services, and handle database errors inside the application
Raise the ALB health check timeout to 120 seconds
objective.explanation: A deep health check that depends on a shared database marks every instance unhealthy at the same time, so the ASG replaces the whole fleet. That turns a short dependency blip into a full outage. The health check should test only whether the instance itself can serve traffic. A 120-second timeout only hides the problem. Removing ELB health checks means hung applications are never detected. Stickiness does nothing for health.

objective.question: A company wants browsers to cache an HTML page for only 60 seconds, so users see updates quickly. CloudFront should cache the same page for one day, and the team will invalidate it when needed. The cache policy TTL settings allow this range. Which header should the origin send?

code.code:
A) Cache-Control: max-age=86400, s-maxage=60
B) Cache-Control: max-age=60, s-maxage=86400
C) Cache-Control: no-cache, max-age=86400
D) Cache-Control: private, max-age=86400

options: B
C
D
A
objective.explanation: Shared caches such as CloudFront use s-maxage, and browsers use max-age. So option B gives 60 seconds in the browser and one day at the edge. Option A reverses the two values. With no-cache, every request must be revalidated. With private, shared caches are told not to store the response.

objective.question: After a web tier is moved behind an Application Load Balancer, the application's audit logs and IP-based rate limiter show only private IP addresses from the VPC instead of real client IPs. What should the developers do?
options: Read the client IP from the X-Forwarded-For header that the ALB adds, and trust only the entries the ALB appended
Turn on ALB stickiness so each client keeps the same source IP
Replace the ALB with a Classic Load Balancer
Enable Proxy Protocol v2 on the ALB target group
objective.explanation: An ALB is a Layer 7 proxy, so it opens a new connection to the target. The original client IP arrives in the X-Forwarded-For header. Proxy Protocol v2 is a Network Load Balancer feature, not an ALB feature. Stickiness does not affect source IPs. A Classic Load Balancer has the same proxy behaviour and is a legacy product.

objective.question: A Node.js API runs behind an Application Load Balancer with the default 60-second idle timeout. The app uses Node's default HTTP keep-alive timeout of 5 seconds. Under light, bursty traffic, the ALB logs a small but steady number of HTTP 502 errors. The targets are healthy and CPU is low. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: Cross-zone load balancing is disabled, so one AZ's targets drop requests. Enable cross-zone load balancing.
The deregistration delay is too short, so in-flight requests are cut off. Increase it to 300 seconds.
The health check interval is too long, so the ALB routes traffic to unhealthy targets. Reduce the interval to 5 seconds.
The ALB reuses idle keep-alive connections to targets, but the app closes them after 5 seconds. Set the app's keep-alive timeout higher than the ALB idle timeout.
objective.explanation: When the backend closes an idle connection first, the ALB can send a request on a socket that is already closed, and the client gets a 502. The backend keep-alive timeout must be longer than the ALB idle timeout. The other options do not match healthy targets, steady traffic and no deployments.

objective.question: This Auto Scaling group is meant to survive the loss of one Availability Zone. During an AZ outage in ap-south-1a, the whole site went down. What is the mistake?

code.code:
WebASG:
  Type: AWS::AutoScaling::AutoScalingGroup
  Properties:
    MinSize: "4"
    MaxSize: "12"
    DesiredCapacity: "4"
    VPCZoneIdentifier:
      - !Ref PrivateSubnetA1   # ap-south-1a
      - !Ref PrivateSubnetA2   # ap-south-1a
    TargetGroupARNs:
      - !Ref WebTG
    HealthCheckType: ELB
    HealthCheckGracePeriod: 120
    LaunchTemplate:
      LaunchTemplateId: !Ref WebLT
      Version: !GetAtt WebLT.LatestVersionNumber

options: Both subnets are in the same AZ, so every instance runs in ap-south-1a. Use subnets in at least two AZs.
MinSize equals DesiredCapacity, which stops the group from replacing failed instances.
The launch template version should be $Default, not the latest version.
HealthCheckType should be EC2, not ELB.
objective.explanation: An Auto Scaling group spreads instances only across the AZs of the subnets you give it. Two subnets in one AZ means zero AZ resilience. ELB health checks are the correct choice, and the other settings do not stop replacement.

objective.question: A company runs a TCP-based trading API in two AWS Regions behind Network Load Balancers. Global clients must allow-list a small, fixed set of IP addresses that never change. Traffic must enter the AWS network close to the user and fail over to the other Region within seconds if one Region becomes unhealthy. Which solution meets ALL requirements?
options: Amazon Route 53 latency-based routing with health checks pointing at the NLBs
An Application Load Balancer in each Region with Elastic IP addresses attached
AWS Global Accelerator with an endpoint group in each Region pointing at the NLBs
Amazon CloudFront with both NLBs as origins in an origin group
objective.explanation: Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IP addresses, brings traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge location, supports arbitrary TCP and UDP, and fails over between Regions using health checks without waiting on DNS caches. CloudFront is for HTTP(S), Route 53 failover depends on DNS TTLs and gives no fixed IPs, and ALBs cannot have Elastic IPs.

objective.question: A new ALB-fronted web tier shows every target as unhealthy. The health check is HTTP on port 80, path /health. The app responds correctly when tested from a bastion host. Based on the instance security group below, what is the cause?

code.code:
Security group: sg-web-instances
Inbound rules:
  Type   Port  Source
  SSH    22    sg-bastion
  HTTP   80    10.20.0.0/24   # bastion subnet
Outbound rules:
  All    All   0.0.0.0/0

ALB security group: sg-alb (in subnets 10.20.10.0/24, 10.20.11.0/24)

options: The instance security group does not allow port 80 from the ALB. Add an inbound rule with source sg-alb.
The health check path must be / because ALB cannot check custom paths.
ALB health checks need ICMP, so an ICMP inbound rule must be added.
Outbound rules must allow port 80 back to the ALB explicitly.
objective.explanation: Health checks and traffic come from the ALB nodes, which are in different subnets from the bastion, so they are blocked. Referencing the ALB security group as the source is the standard fix. Security groups are stateful, so no return-traffic rule is needed, and ALB uses HTTP health checks on any path, not ICMP.

objective.question: A media site on CloudFront serves millions of requests per second. On every viewer request it must redirect /old/* paths to /new/*, add an HSTS header to responses, and normalise the Accept-Language header to improve the cache hit ratio. No network calls are needed. Which option is the MOST cost-effective and lowest latency?
options: CloudFront Functions on the viewer request and viewer response events
An AWS Lambda function behind API Gateway called by the origin
Rewrite rules on the ALB origin with CloudFront caching disabled
Lambda@Edge functions on the origin request and origin response events
objective.explanation: CloudFront Functions are built for lightweight, high-volume viewer request and response logic such as redirects, header changes and cache key normalisation, and they cost less than Lambda@Edge. Lambda@Edge is needed only for network calls, longer run time or origin-side events. Doing the rewrites at the origin adds latency and load.

objective.question: A team moved sessions to an ElastiCache for Redis cluster with replicas in two AZs. The same cluster also caches product catalogue data. During a big sale, users are logged out at random. There was no failover, and the session TTL is 24 hours. Every key in the cluster has a TTL, and the cluster uses the default maxmemory-policy. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The cluster ran out of memory and evicted session keys along with cache keys. Separate sessions from the cache or add memory, and watch the Evictions metric.
The session TTL is too long, so Redis expires keys early to save memory.
The ALB is sending users to different instances because stickiness is disabled.
Redis replication lag is losing session writes during failover.
objective.explanation: The default ElastiCache for Redis policy, volatile-lru, evicts keys that have a TTL when memory is full, and here that includes sessions. Mixing disposable cache data with sessions that must not be lost puts sessions at risk under memory pressure. There was no failover, stickiness does not matter with a shared store, and Redis does not expire keys before their TTL.

objective.question: A stateless API uses JWTs signed by an auth service, valid for 24 hours. Security now requires that a user's access can be revoked within a few minutes after their account is compromised, without giving up most of the benefit of stateless tokens. What is the BEST design?
options: Store every JWT in a database and validate each request against it.
Enable ALB sticky sessions so revocation can be done in instance memory.
Use short-lived access tokens (minutes) with refresh tokens that are checked against a server-side store, and optionally a small denylist of token IDs.
Keep 24-hour tokens and ask users to log out when compromised.
objective.explanation: Short access-token lifetimes bound how long a stolen token works, and the refresh step is a central check where revocation takes effect. A small denylist covers urgent cases. Checking every token in a database removes the stateless benefit, and stickiness brings back server affinity.

objective.question: A company runs a web app in a single Azure region on zone-redundant VM Scale Sets. Traffic comes only from internal users over ExpressRoute. The entry point needs a private IP inside the VNet, path-based routing (/api and /portal to different pools), a Web Application Firewall, TLS termination, and must survive the loss of one availability zone. Which service fits?
options: Azure Traffic Manager with priority routing
Azure Load Balancer Standard with an internal frontend
Azure Application Gateway v2 (WAF_v2 SKU) deployed across availability zones with a private frontend IP
Azure Front Door Premium
objective.explanation: Application Gateway v2 is a regional layer 7 load balancer. It supports a private frontend, path-based routing, WAF, TLS termination and zone redundancy. Front Door is a global edge service for internet-facing apps, Traffic Manager is DNS-based only, and Azure Load Balancer is layer 4 with no path routing or WAF.

objective.question: On Google Cloud, a stateless web tier runs on a zonal managed instance group in us-central1-a behind a global external Application Load Balancer. The architect must survive a full zone outage with no manual action, and keep autoscaling and autohealing. What should they change?
options: Turn on Cloud CDN so cached pages keep the site up during the outage.
Move the instance group to a larger machine type to absorb failures.
Create a second unmanaged instance group in us-central1-b as a cold standby.
Replace it with a regional managed instance group that spreads instances across several zones in us-central1.
objective.explanation: A regional MIG spreads instances across zones in the region and still supports autoscaling and autohealing, so losing one zone leaves serving capacity elsewhere. Unmanaged groups cannot autoscale or autoheal, Cloud CDN covers only cacheable content, and bigger machines do not remove the single-zone dependency.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group uses target tracking on 60% average CPU. The app spends most of its time waiting on downstream API calls. During peaks, p95 latency triples and requests queue up, but CPU stays near 30%, so the group never scales out. What is the BEST change?
options: Switch to target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget, with a target set from load testing.
Move to a larger instance type with more vCPUs.
Add a scheduled action that doubles capacity every hour.
Lower the CPU target to 20%.
objective.explanation: For I/O-bound services, CPU does not reflect load. Requests per target tracks the real demand on each instance. A very low CPU target scales unpredictably, and fixed schedules or bigger instances do not follow the actual traffic.

objective.question:
A team is adding CloudFront in front of an existing public ALB at www.example.com. After the change, the ALB must accept traffic only from CloudFront. Users must see no outage. Which order of steps is correct?
1. Point the www DNS record at the CloudFront distribution.
2. Create the distribution with the ALB as the origin and the correct cache and origin request policies.
3. Restrict the ALB security group to the AWS-managed CloudFront origin-facing prefix list.
4. Test the site through the distribution's own domain name.
objective.explanation: You build and test the distribution before any user depends on it, then move DNS. Locking the ALB down last matters: if you restrict it before the DNS change, users who still resolve straight to the ALB are cut off. Moving DNS first would send users to a distribution that does not exist yet.

objective.question: An Indian e-commerce site runs a flash sale every Friday at 12:00 IST. Traffic jumps 8x within two minutes. Target tracking scaling reacts, but new instances take about 4 minutes to become healthy, so the first minutes are slow. What is the simplest fix?
options: Enable ALB sticky sessions so existing instances keep their users.
Switch the target tracking metric from CPU to memory.
Shorten the ALB health check interval.
Add a scheduled scaling action that raises minimum and desired capacity shortly before 12:00 each Friday.
objective.explanation: When the spike is predictable, pre-scale with a scheduled action so capacity is ready before traffic arrives. Warm pools or predictive scaling can help further. Faster health checks do not speed up boot time, stickiness does not add capacity, and changing the metric does not remove the delay.

objective.question: This Nginx origin sits behind a CDN. The team reports that one user saw another user's account page. What is the mistake?
options: max-age=3600 is too long. Reduce it to 60 seconds.
proxy_pass should use HTTPS so the CDN cannot read the response.
The /account/ pages are personalised but marked public, so shared caches such as the CDN store and serve them to everyone. Use private, no-store.
The /static/ block should not use immutable on versioned files.
objective.explanation: Cache-Control: public allows shared caches to store a personalised response under a cache key that does not include the user, so other users receive it. Personalised pages need private or no-store. A shorter TTL only shrinks the leak window, and the static block is correct for versioned assets.

subjective.question: Why do sticky sessions hurt scaling, and what replaces them?
subjective.answer: Sticky sessions bind a user to one server, usually through a cookie such as AWSALB, because that server holds the session in memory. This causes three problems. First, load becomes uneven: heavy users pile onto some instances, and new instances added by auto scaling get only new users, so scale-out is slow to help. Second, failure loses data: if an instance crashes or is scaled in, every session on it is gone, and users get logged out or lose carts. Third, deployments and draining get harder, because you must wait for sessions to expire. The replacement is to make the web tier stateless. Move session data to a shared store such as ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) or DynamoDB, or keep small signed state on the client, for example a JWT. Then any instance can serve any request. The load balancer can use round robin or least outstanding requests freely, and instances can be added or removed at any time.
keyPoints: Stickiness ties state to one instance, causing uneven load
Instance loss or scale-in destroys sessions
New instances do not absorb existing traffic quickly
Replace with an external session store (ElastiCache, DynamoDB) or signed client tokens
A stateless tier lets the load balancer and auto scaling work freely

subjective.question: Compare vertical and horizontal scaling. When would you still choose vertical scaling?
subjective.answer: Vertical scaling means moving to a bigger machine with more CPU, RAM or network. It needs no code changes, so it is fast. But it keeps a single point of failure, usually needs a restart to resize, and hits a hardware ceiling at the largest instance size. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines behind a load balancer. It gives fault tolerance and near-linear growth, and it works well with auto scaling. However, it needs stateless servers, a load balancer, and care with shared data. I would still choose vertical scaling in a few cases. One is a stateful component that is hard to shard, such as a primary relational database, where a bigger instance buys time. Another is a small internal tool where the extra complexity is not worth it. A third is an emergency, as a quick fix while the team makes the service stateless. In practice, I scale the web tier horizontally and scale databases vertically first, then add read replicas or sharding.
keyPoints: Vertical scaling: simple, but a single point of failure and a hardware ceiling
Horizontal scaling: fault tolerant and elastic, but requires statelessness
Vertical scaling suits hard-to-shard stateful systems such as a primary database
Vertical scaling is acceptable as a short-term fix
Typical pattern: horizontal web tier, vertically scaled data tier at first

subjective.question: Explain the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing, using AWS ALB and NLB as examples.
subjective.answer: An L4 load balancer works at the transport layer. It sees IP addresses, ports and the protocol (TCP, UDP or TLS), but not HTTP content. AWS NLB is the example. It routes connections using flow hashing and gives very low latency, a static IP per AZ, and support for non-HTTP protocols. It suits gaming, IoT, financial feeds, or clients that need fixed IPs to allow-list. An L7 load balancer understands the application protocol. AWS ALB reads HTTP/HTTPS requests, so it can route by path (/api), by host header (admin.example.com), by headers or query strings. It also supports WebSockets, gRPC, redirects, fixed responses, authentication and AWS WAF. The trade-off is that L7 does more work per request, so latency is slightly higher, but you gain far more routing control. Gateway Load Balancer is a third type, used to insert third-party network appliances such as firewalls.
keyPoints: L4 works on IP, port and protocol; L7 inspects HTTP content
NLB: TCP/UDP/TLS, static IP per AZ, ultra-low latency, flow hashing
ALB: path and host routing, WebSockets, gRPC, WAF integration
Choose by protocol, routing needs and latency requirements
Gateway Load Balancer is for network appliances

subjective.question: Round robin versus least connections (least outstanding requests): how does each work, and when does round robin fail?
subjective.answer: Round robin sends each new request to the next target in turn. It is simple, needs no state, and works well when requests cost about the same and targets are identical. It is the ALB default. Least connections, called least outstanding requests on ALB, sends each new request to the target with the fewest requests in flight. Round robin fails when request cost varies widely. For example, a report endpoint may take 20 seconds while a health check takes 5 ms. One server can collect several slow requests and become overloaded while others are idle. It also struggles with mixed instance sizes, and with a newly added instance that is cold. Least outstanding requests adapts to real load in these cases. Its weakness is that a target which fails fast, returning errors quickly, can look 'idle' and attract more traffic. Good health checks therefore matter. ALB also offers weighted random, with optional anomaly mitigation, as a third choice.
keyPoints: Round robin: rotate in turn; best for uniform requests
Least outstanding requests: pick the target with the fewest in-flight requests
Round robin fails with uneven request duration or mixed capacity
Fast-failing targets can attract traffic under least-connections
ALB supports round robin (default), least outstanding requests and weighted random

subjective.question: What is consistent hashing, and why is it better than modulo hashing for a cache cluster?
subjective.answer: With modulo hashing, a key goes to node hash(key) mod N. If N changes from 10 to 11, almost every key maps to a different node. The cache is effectively wiped, and the database gets a stampede of misses. Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a hash ring. Each key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. When a node is added, it takes over only the keys between itself and its predecessor. When a node is removed, only its keys move to the next node. So only about 1/N of keys move. To avoid uneven load, each physical node is given many virtual nodes on the ring. This spreads keys evenly and spreads a failed node's load across many survivors. Consistent hashing is used in DynamoDB-style partitioning, Cassandra, memcached client libraries, and some load balancers. These use it to keep a user or key on the same backend without a lookup table.
keyPoints: Modulo hashing remaps most keys when N changes
On the ring, each key goes to the next node clockwise
Only about 1/N of keys move on a membership change
Virtual nodes improve balance and spread failure load
Prevents cache stampedes during scaling

subjective.question: What does it mean for a service to be stateless, and where should the different kinds of state go?
subjective.answer: A stateless service keeps nothing on the instance that a later request depends on. Any instance can handle any request, and an instance can be killed at any moment without losing data. State still exists; it just lives outside the server. User sessions go to a shared low-latency store such as ElastiCache for Redis or DynamoDB with TTL. Small sessions can also travel with the client as a signed token such as a JWT. Business data goes to a database such as RDS, Aurora or DynamoDB. Uploaded files go to S3, not the local disk. Cached computations go to a distributed cache. Configuration and secrets go to Parameter Store or Secrets Manager, not files baked in by hand. Logs are shipped to CloudWatch or a central system, because the local disk disappears with the instance. A good test: if I terminate a random instance right now, does any user notice anything except, at most, one retried request?
keyPoints: Stateless: no request depends on local instance memory or disk
Sessions go to ElastiCache, DynamoDB or signed client tokens
Files go to S3; data goes to managed databases
Config, secrets and logs are kept outside the instance
Test: terminating any instance causes no user-visible loss

subjective.question: Walk through a web tier design on AWS that survives the loss of one Availability Zone.
subjective.answer: I would use a VPC with public and private subnets in three AZs. Route 53 points to an internet-facing ALB enabled in all three public subnets; ALB nodes run in each AZ, and cross-zone load balancing is on. Behind it, an Auto Scaling group spans the three private subnets and uses ELB health checks, so unhealthy instances are replaced automatically. I size it so two AZs can carry peak load: each AZ holds peak/2, giving 1.5x peak in total. Instances are stateless. Sessions sit in ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ replication, or in DynamoDB. Data sits in Aurora or RDS Multi-AZ. Outbound traffic uses a NAT gateway per AZ, so one AZ failure does not cut egress for the others. Static assets are served from S3 through CloudFront with OAC. If an AZ fails, the ALB stops routing to it, the survivors already have enough capacity, and Auto Scaling rebalances when the AZ returns.
keyPoints: ALB plus an Auto Scaling group across three AZs with ELB health checks
Pre-provision capacity: peak/(N-1) per AZ
Stateless instances; sessions in Multi-AZ ElastiCache or DynamoDB
Multi-AZ database and a NAT gateway per AZ
CloudFront with OAC for static content

subjective.question: Why does a three-AZ deployment need only 1.5x peak capacity to survive one AZ loss, while a two-AZ deployment needs 2x? What are the trade-offs?
subjective.answer: If one of N AZs fails, the remaining N-1 AZs must carry 100% of peak load. So each AZ needs peak/(N-1) capacity. With two AZs, each must hold the full peak, so the total is 2x peak, and half the fleet sits idle in normal times. With three AZs, each holds peak/2, so the total is 1.5x peak, and only one third is spare. With four AZs, the total drops to about 1.33x. More AZs therefore make resilience cheaper, but they add cost elsewhere. You need more subnets and more NAT gateways, cross-AZ data transfer charges rise, and you may need more replicas in the data tier. Some Regions also have limited instance types in certain AZs. Relying on Auto Scaling to replace capacity after the failure is cheaper, but risky. A whole-AZ event creates a rush on capacity in the other AZs, and scaling takes minutes. That is why critical systems pre-provision capacity.
keyPoints: Survivors must carry full peak: peak/(N-1) per AZ
2 AZs = 2x peak; 3 AZs = 1.5x peak
More AZs lower the spare capacity needed but add networking cost and complexity
Reactive scaling after AZ loss is slower and capacity may be scarce
Critical workloads pre-provision spare capacity

subjective.question: How can a CDN help with both static and dynamic content? Give concrete examples using CloudFront.
subjective.answer: For static content such as images, JS, CSS, videos and downloads, CloudFront caches objects at edge locations close to users. This cuts latency and removes most load from the origin. I use long TTLs together with versioned file names. For dynamic content, a CDN still helps in several ways. Content that is personalised but shared by many users, such as a product page or a public API response, can be cached for seconds to minutes ('micro-caching'). Pages that cannot be cached at all still benefit, because the TLS handshake ends at a nearby edge and the request travels to the origin over the AWS backbone with persistent connections. CloudFront also absorbs DDoS traffic with AWS Shield Standard, runs AWS WAF rules, and can run light logic at the edge with CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge, such as redirects, header changes or A/B routing. The origin can be S3 for static content, or an ALB for dynamic content, using separate cache behaviours per path.
keyPoints: Static: edge caching with long TTLs and versioned names
Dynamic: short-TTL micro-caching for shared responses
Uncacheable requests still gain from edge TLS termination and the backbone network
Security at the edge: Shield Standard and WAF
Use path-based cache behaviours with S3 and ALB origins

subjective.question: Explain the cache key and TTL in CloudFront. What goes wrong if you design them badly?
subjective.answer: The cache key decides which requests share one cached object. By default it is the URL path. Through a cache policy you can add specific query strings, headers or cookies. The TTL decides how long an object stays fresh. In CloudFront, the default TTL is 24 hours unless the origin sends Cache-Control or Expires headers, or the cache policy changes it; minimum and maximum TTLs bound what the origin can ask for. A bad key causes two classic failures.
