If it has too much in it, for example all cookies, all headers or a tracking query string, every user gets a unique key, the hit ratio collapses, and the origin takes the full load. If it has too little, for example ignoring a language header that changes the response, users get the wrong content, or even someone else's personalised page. A bad TTL causes stale content when it is too long without versioning, and origin overload when it is too short. Good practice: include only what changes the response, forward other values to the origin with an origin request policy, and version static files.
keyPoints: Cache key = path plus only the query strings, headers and cookies that change the response
Default TTL 24 hours unless Cache-Control or the cache policy says otherwise
Too much in the key leads to a low hit ratio and origin overload
Too little in the key leads to wrong or leaked content
Use origin request policies to forward values without keying on them

subjective.question: What is connection draining (deregistration delay) and how do you make instances shut down gracefully?
subjective.answer: When an instance is deregistered from an ALB target group, for example during scale-in, a deployment or a failed health check, the ALB stops sending it new requests. It keeps existing in-flight requests open for the deregistration delay, which defaults to 300 seconds. This prevents users seeing errors from requests cut off mid-way. I tune the delay to slightly more than the longest normal request. For APIs that finish in a few seconds, 300 seconds just slows deployments. For long uploads or WebSockets, it may need to be longer. Graceful shutdown also needs the application to cooperate. The app should handle SIGTERM, stop accepting new work, finish current requests, flush logs and close database connections. Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks can pause termination while this happens. Health checks should fail fast once shutdown starts. Stateless design makes all of this easy, because nothing on the instance needs to be saved.
keyPoints: Deregistration stops new requests but lets in-flight ones finish
ALB default delay is 300 seconds; tune it to request duration
Too long slows deployments; too short cuts off requests
The app should handle SIGTERM and finish current work
Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks support clean termination

subjective.question: For a stateless tier, should you store sessions in a server-side store like Redis, or in a client-side token like a JWT? Discuss the trade-offs.
subjective.answer: Both remove state from the web servers. A server-side store such as ElastiCache for Redis or DynamoDB keeps only a session ID in a cookie. Its strengths: you can revoke a session at once (logout, ban, password change), store large data such as carts, and keep sensitive data off the client. Its costs: a network lookup on every request, and the store becomes a critical dependency. It must be Multi-AZ and scaled, which Redis replication or DynamoDB give you. A signed JWT carries the claims itself, so any server can verify it with a key and needs no lookup. This scales very well and suits microservices and APIs. Its weaknesses: revocation is hard before expiry, so you use short expiry with refresh tokens or a deny-list. Tokens grow with every claim, and contents are readable unless encrypted. In practice, I use short-lived JWTs for API authentication and Redis or DynamoDB for rich, mutable session data such as carts.
keyPoints: Both make web instances stateless
Server-side store: easy revocation and large data, but a lookup per request and a critical dependency
JWT: no lookup and highly scalable, but hard to revoke and grows in size
Mitigate JWT risks with short expiry, refresh tokens or a deny-list
A common hybrid: JWT for auth plus Redis or DynamoDB for session data

subjective.question: Your consistent-hashing cache cluster still shows one node at 90% CPU while the others sit near 20%. Explain the two different causes this could have and how you would fix each one.
subjective.answer: There are two separate causes. The first is uneven key ranges. With only a few points per node on the ring, one node can own a much larger arc of the hash space, so it gets more keys. The fix is virtual nodes: give each physical node many tokens, for example 100 to 200, so the ring is shared evenly. You can also weight tokens by node capacity. The second cause is a hot key. One celebrity profile or flash-sale item gets a huge share of reads, and every request for it hashes to the same node. More virtual nodes cannot help here. The fixes are a short-TTL local cache in each app server, replicating the hot key under suffixed copies (key#1 to key#N) and reading a random copy, or serving it from the CDN. To tell the two causes apart, look at the per-key request metrics, not just the key counts per node.
keyPoints: Separate an uneven key distribution from a skewed request distribution
Virtual nodes or tokens even out how the ring is shared
Hot keys need local caching, key replication or the CDN
Diagnose with per-key metrics before choosing a fix

subjective.question: Design a web tier on Azure that survives the loss of one availability zone. Name the services and the settings that make each layer zone-resilient.
subjective.answer: At the edge, I use Azure Front Door for TLS termination, WAF and caching. Front Door is global, so a zone failure does not affect it. In the region, an Application Gateway v2 is deployed zone-redundant across zones 1, 2 and 3. Behind it, a Virtual Machine Scale Set is spread across the three zones with zone balancing, plus autoscale rules. With three zones, I size it so that two zones can carry peak load. Session state lives in Azure Cache for Redis Premium or Enterprise with zone redundancy, so the VMs stay stateless. Static files sit in zone-redundant storage (ZRS) and are served through Front Door. The database is Azure SQL or Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server with zone-redundant high availability. Health probes on Application Gateway remove VMs that fail, and the scale set's automatic instance repair replaces them. The key checks are: no single-zone resource is on the request path, and the capacity left after losing a zone covers peak load.
keyPoints: Zone-redundant Application Gateway v2 and a zone-spread VMSS
Externalised session state in zone-redundant Azure Cache for Redis
ZRS storage and a zone-redundant HA database
Size capacity so the remaining zones carry peak load

subjective.question: Review this Terraform for a production web tier. What would fail during an AZ outage or a bad deployment, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: First, vpc_zone_identifier lists only one subnet, so every instance sits in a single AZ. If that AZ fails, the whole tier goes down. I would add private subnets in at least two, and preferably three, AZs. Second, health_check_type is EC2. The ASG then replaces only instances whose status checks fail, not instances whose application has hung. Setting it to ELB, with a sensible grace period, lets ALB health checks drive replacement. Third, min_size of 1 and max_size of 4 are too low for production. Minimum capacity should cover one AZ failing, and the maximum should leave room above peak. I would also add a target-tracking scaling policy. Fourth, using version $Latest means any launch template change rolls out with no control. I would pin the version and use instance refresh, with a minimum healthy percentage, or blue-green deployment. Finally, I would check that the target group has a suitable deregistration delay.
keyPoints: Single subnet means a single AZ, which is a single point of failure
Use ELB health checks so application failures are detected
Set min and max capacity for AZ loss and for peak load, with a scaling policy
Pin the launch template version and use controlled instance refresh

subjective.question: How do you load-balance and scale a service with long-lived WebSocket connections? What changes compared with short HTTP requests?
subjective.answer: With WebSockets, each connection stays pinned to one backend for minutes or hours. The load balancer balances connections, not requests. ALB supports WebSockets, and NLB works at Layer 4 for very high connection counts. Round robin can leave old instances overloaded after a scale-out, because new instances only receive new connections. So I watch connections per instance and scale on that metric. During scale-in or deployment, deregistration delay is not enough by itself. The server should send a close or reconnect message, and clients should reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a reconnect storm. Any state a connection needs, such as subscriptions or presence, goes in a shared store like Redis. A pub/sub layer fans messages out to whichever node holds the user's socket. With that in place, any node can accept a reconnect, so the tier stays stateless in practice even though connections are sticky.
keyPoints: Connections, not requests, are the unit of load
New nodes start empty, so scale on connection count and rebalance through reconnects
Graceful close with jittered client reconnects during scale-in
Shared state and pub/sub keep nodes replaceable

subjective.question: A product team wants to cache API responses at the CDN to cut origin load. Some responses are the same for everyone, some vary by country, and some are per user. How do you cache safely without leaking one user's data to another?
subjective.answer: I classify every endpoint first. Public responses, such as a product catalogue, can be cached with a short TTL using s-maxage. I keep the cache key small, using only the query parameters that change the response. Country-specific responses can be cached by adding the CloudFront-Viewer-Country header to the cache key. That gives a few hundred variants at most, not millions. Per-user responses must not be cached at the shared edge. The origin sends Cache-Control: private or no-store, and the cache behavior for those paths uses a caching-disabled policy. CloudFront still helps there through TLS termination near the user and persistent connections to the origin. The main risk is someone caching a response that depends on the Authorization header or a session cookie when that value is not in the cache key. That serves user A's data to user B. I prevent this with separate path patterns, default deny for caching, and tests that compare responses for two users.
keyPoints: Classify endpoints as public, by segment, or personalised
Put only the varying dimensions in the cache key
Mark personalised responses private or no-store, with caching disabled
The biggest risk is auth-dependent responses cached without auth in the key

subjective.question: One AZ fails. Your remaining instances suddenly get 50% more traffic, latency spikes, and clients start retrying, which makes things worse. Explain what is happening and how you would design to prevent it.
subjective.answer: This is a cascading overload. The surviving instances get the failed AZ's share of traffic. Autoscaling takes minutes to launch and warm new instances. Meanwhile, timeouts trigger client retries, so load grows further. The first defence is static stability: pre-provision enough capacity that the remaining AZs can carry peak load without needing to scale. Second, cut the scaling lag with target tracking at a moderate target, for example 50–60% CPU, plus faster-booting images, and EC2 warm pools where startup is slow. Third, control retries: use exponential backoff with jitter, a retry budget, and circuit breakers in clients and SDKs. Fourth, protect the servers with load shedding and rate limiting. They should return quick 503s instead of queueing until everything times out. CDN caching of static and cacheable content also takes load off the origin. I would test this with a game-day exercise or an AWS Fault Injection Service experiment.
keyPoints: Failover traffic plus retries plus slow scaling equals a cascade
Static stability: pre-provision for one AZ loss
Exponential backoff with jitter, retry budgets and circuit breakers
Load shedding, plus testing with fault injection

subjective.question: You inherit a legacy Java app that keeps sessions in memory and depends on ALB sticky sessions. Describe a step-by-step migration to a stateless tier with no user-facing downtime.
subjective.answer: Step one, audit what goes into the session: login identity, cart, CSRF tokens, cached objects. Also look for local files such as uploads or temporary reports. Step two, move uploads to S3 and remove cached data that can be rebuilt. Step three, add a shared session store. For Java, Spring Session with ElastiCache for Redis OSS or Valkey lets you swap the store without rewriting business logic. Make session objects serialisable and small. Step four, roll this out while stickiness is still on. New sessions are written to Redis, and users see no change. You can also dual-read: check Redis first, then local memory. Step five, once old in-memory sessions have expired, turn off stickiness and switch the algorithm to least outstanding requests. Step six, prove it works by terminating instances under load and checking that no user is logged out. Then enable aggressive scale-in and faster deployments.
keyPoints: Audit session contents and local disk use first
Move files to S3 and sessions to a shared store like Redis
Keep stickiness on during the cutover, then remove it once old sessions expire
Validate by killing instances under load

subjective.question: Case study: A Hindi news portal gets about 5,000 requests per second normally and 50x that within minutes when breaking news hits. 95% of traffic is anonymous readers. Logged-in users can comment. The origin is a stateless app tier on EC2 with an RDS database. Design the web tier and explain how each part handles the spike.
subjective.answer: Most of the load is anonymous reads, so I put CloudFront in front and treat it as the main serving layer. Article pages for anonymous users get a short TTL, say 30–60 seconds, with stale-while-revalidate. Even a 30-second TTL turns hundreds of thousands of requests into a handful of origin hits per edge. I keep cookies out of the cache key for anonymous paths and send /comments and /login to a no-cache behaviour. I would turn on Origin Shield so edges collapse their misses into one regional request. Behind it, an ALB and an Auto Scaling group spread across three AZs, scaling on request count per target, with a higher minimum during news hours. Sessions go to Multi-AZ ElastiCache. Comment writes are queued in SQS so a write burst cannot overload RDS, and reads use read replicas. I load-test the 50x case, because the CDN hit ratio decides whether the origin survives.
keyPoints: The CDN is the main defence for read-heavy spikes: short TTLs, a clean cache key, request collapsing and Origin Shield
Separate cacheable anonymous paths from personalised or write paths using different cache behaviours
Multi-AZ stateless tier scaling on request count per target, with sessions in Multi-AZ Redis
Buffer writes with a queue and offload reads to replicas to protect the database

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: You moved sessions from instance memory to a shared Redis cluster and turned off ALB stickiness. Users are still logged out at random when a request lands on a different instance. Redis shows the session keys exist. What could cause this, and how do you find out?
subjective.answer: If the keys exist in Redis but some instances cannot use them, the problem is usually per-instance configuration, not storage. The most common cause is that each instance generates its own session-signing or encryption secret at startup. Instance A signs the cookie, and instance B rejects the signature and starts a new session. The fix is one shared secret, loaded from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, used by every instance. The second cause is different settings across versions during a rolling deploy, such as session key prefix, serializer or cookie name, so old and new instances cannot read each other's sessions. The third is cookie scope: a wrong Domain or Path attribute, or the Secure flag combined with HTTP somewhere in the chain. To diagnose, I log the instance ID and session ID on each request, decode the cookie, and compare app config across instances. Then I send two requests from one client to two known instances and see which one rejects the session.
keyPoints: Per-instance signing or encryption secrets are the classic cause; store one shared secret centrally
Mixed app versions with different session prefixes or serializers during a rolling deploy
Cookie attribute issues: Domain, Path, Secure flag, cookie name
Diagnose by logging instance ID and session ID and testing requests against two known instances

subjective.question: Comparison: A partner integration needs your HTTPS API to be reachable on fixed IP addresses they can allow-list, and you also need path-based routing to several microservices. Compare (a) an NLB with an ALB as its target and (b) AWS Global Accelerator in front of an ALB. Which would you choose and why?
subjective.answer: Both keep the ALB for layer 7 path routing and add a layer that has fixed IPs. With an NLB that uses an ALB as its target, the NLB gets a static IP or Elastic IP in each AZ, and it forwards TCP to the ALB, which does the routing. This is regional, cheap and simple. The cost is one extra hop, and a client-IP pass-through that needs thinking about. Global Accelerator gives two static anycast IPs that are the same worldwide. It brings traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge, can target the ALB directly, keeps the client IP, and can fail over between Regions using health checks. It costs more because of a fixed hourly fee plus data transfer premiums. If the partners are in one country and the API is in one Region, I would choose NLB plus ALB. If partners are global, latency matters, or I need multi-Region failover, I would choose Global Accelerator.
keyPoints: ALB does the layer 7 routing in both designs; the front layer only supplies fixed IPs
NLB with ALB target: per-AZ static IPs, regional, cheaper, one extra hop
Global Accelerator: two global anycast IPs, edge entry, multi-Region failover, client IP preserved, higher cost
Choose based on where partners are and whether you need multi-Region

subjective.question: Ordering a procedure: You must run a game day that proves your web tier survives the loss of one AZ. List the steps in order, from preparation to follow-up.
subjective.answer: First, define the hypothesis and success criteria, for example: with one AZ gone, error rate stays under 0.5% and p95 latency under 500 ms, with no manual action. Second, check the prerequisites: dashboards and alarms for each AZ, current capacity against N+1 sizing, and a rollback or abort plan agreed with stakeholders. Third, start in staging, or in production at low traffic with a small blast radius. Fourth, inject the failure with AWS Fault Injection Service, for example by stopping instances in one AZ or disrupting that AZ's subnet connectivity. Fifth, watch what happens: ALB marking targets unhealthy, the Auto Scaling group rebalancing, Redis or RDS failing over, and client-facing errors. Sixth, end the experiment, or let the stop conditions end it, and confirm full recovery and rebalancing. Finally, hold a blameless review, record gaps such as slow failover, missing alarms or retry storms, fix them, and schedule the next run.
keyPoints: Start with a measurable hypothesis and stop conditions
Verify observability, capacity headroom and an abort plan before injecting faults
Inject the AZ failure in a controlled way, for example with AWS Fault Injection Service, and observe every layer
Confirm recovery, then review and fix the gaps found

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes: This Nginx config load-balances a stateless web tier. What is wrong for a horizontally scaled, fault-tolerant tier, and how would you fix it?
subjective.answer: First, ip_hash pins each client IP to one server. That is stickiness by another name, and it is uneven: a large office or mobile carrier NAT sends thousands of users through one IP, so one server gets hot. A stateless tier should use least_conn or plain round robin. Second, the server list is hard-coded. New instances from autoscaling never get traffic, and dead ones are not removed except through passive max_fails checks. I would replace this with a managed load balancer such as an ALB in front of an Auto Scaling group, or use dynamic service discovery. Third, all three IPs look like they are in one subnet, 10.0.1.x, which suggests one AZ. Spread backends across AZs. Fourth, a 600-second read timeout lets slow requests hold connections for a long time. Set it close to the real worst-case response time. Also add X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto headers, and listen on 443 with TLS.
keyPoints: ip_hash is IP-based affinity; behind NAT it causes hot spots, so use least_conn or round robin
A static server list cannot follow autoscaling; use a managed load balancer or service discovery
All backends in one subnet means one AZ; spread them across AZs
Unbounded timeouts, missing forwarded headers and no TLS

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: Your CloudFront hit ratio is 97%, yet every few minutes the origin gets a sharp spike of identical requests that briefly pushes ALB latency up. The spikes line up with the TTL of your most popular pages. Explain the cause and the fixes.
subjective.answer: This is a cache stampede. When a hot object expires, many edge locations miss at about the same moment, and each one asks the origin for the same object. The average hit ratio looks fine, but the misses arrive in bursts. CloudFront already collapses simultaneous requests for the same key within one cache, but different edges and regional caches still each go to the origin. Fixes: turn on Origin Shield so all edges funnel misses through one regional layer, which leaves roughly one origin fetch per object. Have the origin send stale-while-revalidate, and stale-if-error, so edges keep serving the old copy while one refresh runs in the background. Add small random jitter to TTLs, or stagger the publishing times of hot objects, so they do not all expire together. Inside the app, use request coalescing or a lock in the application cache so one worker rebuilds the page while the others wait or serve stale content.
keyPoints: Synchronised expiry of hot objects causes bursts of misses: a cache stampede or thundering herd
Origin Shield centralises misses from all edges
stale-while-revalidate and stale-if-error keep serving while refreshing
TTL jitter and app-level request coalescing spread out or merge rebuilds

subjective.question: Comparison: A product-recommendation service keeps a large in-process cache of each user's model features, which takes 2 seconds to load from storage. Should its load balancer use least-request or consistent-hash (ring hash) routing on user ID? Justify your choice and its risks.
subjective.answer: This is one of the few cases where consistent hashing is justified. The service is stateless for correctness, because any instance can serve any user, but it is not stateless for performance, because a cache miss costs 2 seconds. Ring-hash routing on user ID sends each user to the same instance, so cache hits rise sharply and memory is used well, since each user's data sits on one node instead of all of them. When an instance is added or removed, only about 1/N of users move. The risks: hot users or a skewed key distribution overload one node, so use virtual nodes and a bounded-load variant if your proxy supports it. Scaling events and deployments still cause warm-up misses. A node failure sends its users to a neighbour that is cold. Least-request balances load better and is simpler, but most requests would miss the cache. I would choose ring hash with bounded load and keep health-based ejection.
keyPoints: Stateless for correctness but stateful for performance, so affinity pays off here
Consistent hashing raises the local cache hit rate and moves only about 1/N of keys on resize
Risks: hot keys, uneven load, cold caches after failures and scaling
Mitigate with virtual nodes, bounded-load hashing and health ejection; least-request is right when there is no local cache

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: An Auto Scaling group keeps flapping. It scales out from 4 to 10 instances, then back to 4 a few minutes later, then out again, all during steady traffic. What causes this and how do you stop it?
subjective.answer: Flapping means the scaling signal reacts to the scaling itself. Common causes are these. Newly launched instances are counted in the group metric before they are warm. They report low CPU while booting, the average drops, and scale-in starts. The fix is to set the default instance warm-up so new instances are left out of the metric until they are ready. Another cause is having separate scale-out and scale-in step policies with thresholds too close together, for example out at 60% and in at 55%, with no gap between them. Use one target tracking policy, which scales in more cautiously, or widen the gap. A third cause is a noisy metric with a short period. Use a longer evaluation period or a smoother metric such as requests per target. Also check that health check failures are not terminating and replacing instances, because that looks like flapping too. Finally, set a sensible minimum capacity for the steady load.
keyPoints: Booting instances skew the metric unless a warm-up period excludes them
Scale-out and scale-in thresholds too close together; prefer target tracking
Noisy or short-period metrics trigger repeated actions
Rule out health-check replacement loops and set a sensible minimum

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes: This Express service is about to be placed in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB. Which lines break statelessness or horizontal scaling, and where should each piece of state go?
subjective.answer: There are four problems. First, express-session uses the default in-memory store, so sessions live on one instance and are lost on scale-in. Use a shared store such as connect-redis on Multi-AZ ElastiCache. Second, the secret is random on each instance, so cookies signed by one instance fail on another. Load one secret from Secrets Manager. Third, uploads go to the local disk at /var/app/uploads, so GET /last fails whenever it hits a different instance, and files disappear when instances are replaced. Upload to S3, ideally with presigned URLs so files skip the app, and store only the object key. Fourth, rateCounts is a per-process object. Limits are multiplied by the number of instances and reset on restart. Use Redis counters or AWS WAF rate-based rules. Also, req.ip is the ALB's private IP unless trust proxy is set, so every client shares one counter. After these fixes, any instance can serve any request.
keyPoints: The in-memory session store loses sessions; use a shared Redis store
A per-instance random secret breaks cookie validation; use one central secret
Local disk uploads cause cross-instance misses and data loss; use S3
An in-process rate limiter is wrong across instances; use Redis or WAF, and set trust proxy for the real client IP

subjective.question: Ordering a procedure: Describe, step by step, a blue/green release of a stateless web tier using ALB weighted target groups, including how you roll back.
subjective.answer: Step 1: Build the green environment, a new Auto Scaling group and target group running the new version, across the same AZs. Size it for full traffic. Step 2: Confirm the two versions can run side by side: the same session store, a compatible session format, and backward-compatible database schema changes already applied. Step 3: Wait for green targets to pass health checks, and run smoke tests through a test listener rule, such as a header-based rule, before real users arrive. Step 4: Change the listener's forward action weights, for example 95 to blue and 5 to green. Watch error rates, latency and business metrics. Step 5: Increase step by step, 25, 50, then 100, pausing at each step. Step 6: To roll back at any point, set blue back to 100. This is instant because blue is still running. Step 7: After a bake period, scale blue down. Note that target group stickiness, if enabled, holds users on one colour.
keyPoints: Build green fully sized, across AZs, with the same shared session store
Apply schema changes in a backward-compatible way before switching
Shift traffic gradually using listener weights and watch metrics at each step
Instant rollback by restoring weights; remove blue only after a bake period

subjective.question: Comparison: A paid video-learning site serves course videos from S3 through CloudFront. Only enrolled users may watch. Compare CloudFront signed URLs and signed cookies for this case, and say which you would use.
subjective.answer: Both let CloudFront check access at the edge with a signature from a trusted key group, so the origin and the app servers are not hit for each video request, which keeps the tier stateless. A signed URL covers one file, or a wildcard pattern with a custom policy, and works with any client, including apps that cannot hold cookies. Signed cookies cover many files at once, which suits adaptive streaming such as HLS or DASH, where one video is a playlist plus hundreds of segment files. Signing each segment URL is painful, and the playlist would have to be rewritten. For streamed course videos, I would use signed cookies scoped to the course path, with an expiry of a few hours, issued after the app checks enrolment. I would use signed URLs for single downloads such as PDFs, or for clients that cannot send cookies. In both cases, use origin access control so S3 cannot be reached directly, and keep expiries short.
keyPoints: Both verify access at the edge, so the origin is not involved on each request
Signed URL: one object or pattern, works without cookies
Signed cookies: many objects, ideal for HLS or DASH segments under a path
Combine with origin access control and short expiries

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: After you put CloudFront in front of an existing web app, login stops working. Users submit the form and land back on the login page, and API calls return 401. Direct access to the ALB works. What went wrong, and how do you configure CloudFront correctly?
subjective.answer: CloudFront sends the origin only the headers, cookies and query strings that the cache policy and origin request policy allow. With a default caching policy, it drops the session cookie and the Authorization header, so the app never sees the user's credentials. Worse, a login redirect or a 401 might be cached and served to other users. The fix is separate cache behaviours. Use a static behaviour for /assets/* with long TTLs and no cookies in the cache key. Use a dynamic behaviour for /login, /account/* and /api/* with the managed CachingDisabled cache policy and an origin request policy that forwards all viewer headers and cookies, or AllViewerExceptHostHeader, which includes Authorization. Allow all HTTP methods, including POST, on the dynamic behaviour. Check that the app's cookie Domain matches the public hostname. Then test the login flow with the response headers that show whether each request was a CloudFront hit or miss.
keyPoints: The default cache policy strips cookies and Authorization from origin requests
Use separate cache behaviours for static and dynamic paths
Dynamic paths: CachingDisabled, forward cookies and headers via an origin request policy, allow POST
Check cookie domain and test with the cache hit or miss response headers

subjective.question: Case study: A cricket-ticketing platform in India opens sales for a final at 10:00 AM. Two million users arrive within one minute for 60,000 seats. The stateless web tier can scale, but the booking database cannot handle more than a few thousand writes per second. How do you design the front of the system to stay up and treat users fairly?
subjective.answer: The bottleneck is seat inventory, not web servers, so I control how fast users are admitted. First, a virtual waiting room at the edge. Users arriving before 10:00 get a static waiting page from the CDN. At opening, each user gets a signed token with a random or arrival-based queue position, and the token is checked at the edge by CloudFront Functions. Only tokens that have been admitted can reach the booking APIs, and admissions are released at a rate the database can absorb. Second, pre-scale the web tier and the session store across three AZs with scheduled scaling, because autoscaling is too slow for a one-minute spike. Third, put WAF rate-based rules and bot control in front to stop scalpers. Fourth, make seat holds short-lived reservations with a TTL in Redis, committed to the database only at payment, using idempotency keys. Serve the seat map from cache with seconds-level freshness. Keep the user informed with queue position, so they do not retry and add load.
keyPoints: Control admission with an edge waiting room and signed queue tokens
Pre-scale the stateless tier and session store across AZs; autoscaling is too slow
WAF rate limiting and bot protection for fairness
Short-TTL seat holds, idempotent payment commits and cached seat maps to protect the database

steps.overview: This step teaches how to put a cache in front of a database so that reads become fast and cheap. It covers the four caching patterns, the eviction policies, and the three classic failure modes: stampede, hot keys and penetration. All three cloud architect exams test this through scenario questions, for example 'reduce read latency on RDS' (ElastiCache), 'microsecond reads on DynamoDB' (DAX) or 'Azure Cache for Redis vs CDN'. Interviews expect you to defend the trade-off between consistency and speed.
objectives: Implement a cache-aside layer for a read-heavy product page with TTLs and invalidation on write
Compare cache-aside, read-through, write-through and write-behind on consistency, latency and data-loss risk
Choose an eviction policy (LRU, LFU, TTL-based) and explain when each one wins
Diagnose and fix cache stampede, hot keys and cache penetration
Justify Redis or Memcached (or ElastiCache/DAX/Azure Cache for Redis) for a given scenario

concepts.explanation: The application checks the cache first. On a miss, it reads the database, writes the result into the cache with a TTL, and returns it. Only data that is actually requested gets cached, and a cache failure does not break reads. The downsides are a slow first request (miss penalty) and possible stale data until the TTL expires or the key is invalidated.

The cache itself loads missing data from the database through a configured loader, so the application only talks to the cache. The behaviour is the same as cache-aside, but the loading logic lives in the cache layer or library. DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a managed read-through and write-through cache for DynamoDB.

Every write goes to the cache and the database synchronously, and the write succeeds only when both are updated. Cache reads are always fresh, but each write is slower and the cache fills with data that may never be read. Pair it with a TTL to limit wasted memory.

Writes go to the cache and are acknowledged immediately. The cache flushes them to the database asynchronously, often in batches. This gives very low write latency and absorbs write bursts. The risk is data loss if the cache node fails before the flush, so you need persistence or replication and you must accept eventual consistency.

LRU removes the key that was used least recently. It suits workloads where recent items are likely to be read again. LFU removes the key with the fewest accesses, which protects long-term popular keys from a one-off scan. TTL expires a key after a fixed time whether or not memory is full. TTL controls staleness, while LRU and LFU control memory.

A popular key expires and thousands of requests miss at the same moment, so all of them hit the database. Fixes: a mutex or single-flight lock so only one request rebuilds the key, TTL jitter so keys do not expire together, early probabilistic refresh before expiry, and serving the stale value while one worker refreshes it.

One key receives so much traffic that the single shard holding it becomes the bottleneck, even when the rest of the cluster is idle. Fixes: a small in-process local cache in front of Redis, replicating the key under suffixed names (key#1..key#N) and reading one at random, and adding read replicas for reads.

Requests for keys that do not exist (often from bots or attacks) always miss the cache and always hit the database. Fixes: cache a null or empty result with a short TTL (negative caching), check membership with a Bloom filter before querying, and validate input IDs at the edge.

Redis offers rich data structures (hashes, sorted sets, streams), replication, persistence (RDB/AOF), pub/sub, Lua scripting and cluster sharding. Memcached is a simple multi-threaded key-value store with no persistence or replication, and it scales vertically across CPU cores easily. Choose Redis when you need HA, persistence, leaderboards or sessions with failover. Choose Memcached for a plain, disposable object cache.

keyFacts: Exam trigger: 'read-heavy RDS, reduce latency/cost' → Amazon ElastiCache (cache-aside). 'DynamoDB, microsecond reads, minimal code change' → DAX.
ElastiCache engines are Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached. Only the Redis OSS/Valkey engines support replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, backups and persistence.
Memcached is multi-threaded and has no replication or persistence. A lost node means its cached data is gone, which is acceptable for a pure cache.
Open-source Redis defaults to maxmemory-policy noeviction, so writes fail when memory is full. ElastiCache's default parameter group uses volatile-lru. Always set the policy deliberately.
Redis eviction policies: noeviction, allkeys-lru, volatile-lru, allkeys-lfu, volatile-lfu, allkeys-random, volatile-random, volatile-ttl. The volatile-* policies only evict keys that have a TTL.
Decision rule: read-heavy and stale-tolerant → cache-aside with a TTL. Read-after-write freshness needed → write-through (plus a TTL). Write-heavy and some loss tolerable → write-behind.
On update in cache-aside, delete the cache key after writing the database. Do not try to update it in place. Deletion is idempotent and avoids racing writers storing out-of-order values.
Always add random jitter (for example ±10%) to TTLs to prevent mass expiry and stampedes.
Azure Cache for Redis and GCP Memorystore (Redis/Valkey, Memcached) are the equivalent managed services on AZ-305 and Professional Cloud Architect.

example.caption: Cache-aside for a product page with TTL jitter, negative caching and a stampede lock (redis-py)

pitfalls: Caching without a TTL. A single missed invalidation then serves stale data forever. Always set a TTL as a safety net.
Updating the cache value on write instead of deleting it. Two concurrent writers can leave the older value in the cache. Delete it, or use versioning.
Picking write-behind for financial or order data. If the cache node fails before the flush, you lose acknowledged writes. The exam expects write-through or direct DB writes here.
Choosing Memcached when the question mentions high availability, failover, persistence, sorted sets or pub/sub. Those features point to Redis/Valkey.
Using a volatile-* eviction policy when most keys have no TTL. Redis then cannot evict anything and writes start failing with OOM errors.
Treating the cache as the source of truth. The database must remain authoritative, and the system must still work (only slower) if the cache is flushed.

workflow.title: Cache-aside request flow for a product page

steps.label: Check cache by key
steps.detail: The app runs GET product:{id} against Redis and returns the value immediately on a hit.

steps.label: Handle miss with lock
steps.detail: On a miss, one request acquires a short SET NX lock so that only it queries the database.

steps.label: Read from database
steps.detail: The lock holder reads the row from the primary database, not a lagging replica, to avoid caching stale data.

steps.label: Populate with jittered TTL
steps.detail: It stores the row (or a null marker with a short TTL) using a randomised TTL, then releases the lock.

steps.label: Invalidate on write
steps.detail: Every update writes the database first and then deletes the cache key, so the next read reloads fresh data.

steps.label: Monitor and tune
steps.detail: Track hit ratio, evictions, memory and hot-key traffic, then adjust TTLs, eviction policy and node size.

project.title: product-cache-aside
project.summary: A Node.js product page API that reads products from PostgreSQL through a Redis cache-aside layer. It also guards against cache stampede (lock), cache penetration (negative caching plus input checks) and hot keys (a 1-second in-process L1 cache). docker-compose.yml and init.sql give you Redis with LRU eviction and a seeded database. src/db.js is the slow source of truth. src/cache.js holds the caching patterns and fixes. src/server.js wires reads and writes, using delete-on-write invalidation. README.md lists three ways the cache serves stale data and defends a pattern choice for read-heavy and write-heavy workloads.

docker compose up -d
npm install
npm start
curl localhost:3000/products/1
curl -X PUT localhost:3000/products/1 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"price_inr":1299}'
for i in $(seq 1 50); do curl -s localhost:3000/products/2 > /dev/null & done; wait
curl localhost:3000/stats

files.code:
# Local infra: Redis (cache) + PostgreSQL (source of truth)
services:
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
      - "6379:6379"
    # Small memory cap so eviction is real. allkeys-lru evicts the least recently used key.
    # Try allkeys-lfu for hot/cold traffic, or volatile-ttl to evict keys closest to expiry first.
    command: ["redis-server", "--maxmemory", "64mb", "--maxmemory-policy", "allkeys-lru"]
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: shop
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: shop
      POSTGRES_DB: shop
    volumes:
      # Runs once on first start to create and seed the products table
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql:ro

-- Source of truth for the product page
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS products (
  id         INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name       TEXT        NOT NULL,
  price_inr  INTEGER     NOT NULL,
  stock      INTEGER     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

INSERT INTO products (id, name, price_inr, stock) VALUES
  (1, 'Cotton Kurta',        999, 40),
  (2, 'Steel Water Bottle',  449, 120),
  (3, 'Wireless Earbuds',   1999, 15),
  (4, 'Masala Tea 500g',     299, 300)
ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING;

# product-cache-aside (Step 3: Caching)

Flow: GET /products/:id -> L1 (1 s) -> Redis -> on a miss, one caller takes a lock -> PostgreSQL -> Redis (TTL + jitter).
Writes: update PostgreSQL, then DEL the Redis key (cache-aside invalidation).

## What each fix maps to
- Stampede (thundering herd): `SET lock:key NX PX` lets one caller rebuild; others wait. TTL jitter avoids mass expiry at one moment.
- Penetration (lookups for ids that do not exist): input validation plus a short-TTL `__NULL__` marker. At large scale, add a Bloom filter.
- Hot key: a 1-second in-process L1 cache. Other options are key replicas (`product:1#0..N`) or read replicas.
- Eviction: `allkeys-lru` in docker-compose.yml. Use LFU when a small set of keys stays popular for a long time. TTL bounds staleness.

## Three ways this cache serves stale data
1. **TTL window.** Someone changes the DB directly (an admin SQL script or another service) and skips `invalidate`. Readers then see the old price until the TTL (300 s + jitter) expires.
2. **Read/write race.** Reader A misses and reads the old row. Writer B updates the DB and deletes the key. A then writes the old row into Redis. The stale value lives for a full TTL. Fixes: a delayed second delete, versioned values, or a short TTL.
3. **L1 and failed deletes.** Each app instance keeps its own L1 copy for up to 1 s after a write on another instance. Also, if `redis.del` fails after the DB commit, the old value stays until its TTL expires. Fixes: retry the delete, or use CDC (change data capture) or pub/sub invalidation.

## Checkpoint: picking a pattern
- **Read-heavy** (product page, about 100:1 reads to writes): use cache-aside + TTL + delete-on-write. Only requested data is cached. A cache outage degrades to the DB. A little staleness is acceptable.
- **Write-heavy** (view counters, likes): use write-behind. Write to Redis (for example `INCR`) and flush to the DB in batches. This cuts DB writes, but you can lose data if the cache dies before the flush.
- **Write-through** fits when reads must see a write at once and writes are moderate. Every write updates the cache and the DB together, so the cache is fresh but each write is slower.
- **Read-through** is the same as cache-aside, except the cache library or provider does the loading for you.

## Redis vs Memcached
- **Redis:** rich data types, persistence, replication, Lua scripting and pub/sub. It suits locks, counters and leaderboards. The managed services are ElastiCache/MemoryDB, Memorystore and Azure Cache for Redis.
- **Memcached:** simple multithreaded key/value store with no persistence. It suits plain, scale-out object caching.

revision.examFocus: On SAA-C03, caching sits mainly in the high-performing architectures domain, with spill-over into resilience (Multi-AZ Redis/Valkey) and cost (offloading RDS reads). Questions are short scenarios where you pick ElastiCache vs DAX vs read replicas vs CloudFront, or Redis/Valkey vs Memcached, from wording like 'microsecond', 'failover' or 'session'. AZ-305 (Azure Cache for Redis) and Professional Cloud Architect (Memorystore) test the same ideas inside case studies, while interviews probe patterns, invalidation, stampedes and hot keys.

compare.difference: ElastiCache is a general cache that your application code fills and invalidates, for any data source such as RDS or APIs. DAX is a read-through/write-through cache built only for DynamoDB and is API-compatible, so code changes are minimal.
compare.chooseA: Pick ElastiCache when the backend is RDS/Aurora, the cache holds computed results or sessions, or you need Redis data structures.
compare.chooseB: Pick DAX when the table is DynamoDB and the question says microsecond reads with minimal application change.

compare.difference: Redis/Valkey gives replication, Multi-AZ failover, backups, persistence and rich types (sorted sets, hashes, streams, pub/sub). Memcached is a simple multi-threaded key-value store with no replication or persistence.
compare.chooseA: Pick Redis/Valkey for any mention of high availability, failover, durability, leaderboards, session data you cannot lose, or pub/sub.
compare.chooseB: Pick Memcached only for a plain, disposable object cache where simplicity and multi-threaded scaling on large nodes are the stated goals.

compare.difference: Write-through writes to the cache and the database in the same request, so reads are fresh and nothing acknowledged is lost, but writes are slower. Write-behind acknowledges after the cache write and flushes to the database later, so writes are fast but data can be lost if the cache fails.
compare.chooseA: Pick write-through when reads must see the latest write or the data is financial, orders or inventory.
compare.chooseB: Pick write-behind for very high write rates where losing a few updates is acceptable, such as counters, view stats or telemetry.

compare.difference: In cache-aside the application checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and stores the result. In read-through the cache or a library loads from the database itself, so the app only talks to the cache.
compare.chooseA: Pick cache-aside for most ElastiCache answers: only requested data is cached and the app keeps working if the cache is down.
compare.chooseB: Pick read-through when a managed layer (like DAX) or a caching library owns loading and you want simpler application code.

compare.difference: A cache serves repeated identical reads in sub-millisecond time and cuts database cost. Read replicas scale SQL queries with millisecond latency and need no cache invalidation logic.
compare.chooseA: Pick ElastiCache when the same queries or objects are read again and again and the question says lowest latency or reduce database load and cost.
compare.chooseB: Pick read replicas when reads are varied or ad-hoc, such as reporting queries, or the question says no application code changes.

cues.cue: Store user sessions so web servers can be stateless behind a load balancer
cues.pick: ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey (or DynamoDB)
cues.why: A shared, fast and replicated session store lets any instance serve any user and survives a node failure.

cues.cue: Real-time leaderboard or ranking
cues.pick: Redis/Valkey sorted sets
cues.why: Sorted sets give ranking operations natively, and Memcached has no such data type.

cues.cue: Database CPU spikes every time popular keys expire at once
cues.pick: Cache stampede fixes: TTL jitter, single-flight lock or request coalescing, early background refresh
cues.why: These fixes stop many concurrent misses for the same key from all hitting the database together.

cues.cue: Bots request random or non-existent product IDs and every request hits the database
cues.pick: Cache penetration fixes: cache negative (null) results with a short TTL, Bloom filter, input validation
cues.why: Misses for keys that never exist can never be cached normally, so you must cache the 'not found' result or block the request early.

cues.cue: One celebrity or flash-sale key overloads a single cache shard
cues.pick: Hot-key fixes: local in-process cache, replicate the key across shards (key suffixes), read replicas
cues.why: Spreading or locally absorbing reads of one key removes the single-node bottleneck.

cues.cue: Static images or pages for users around the world
cues.pick: Amazon CloudFront (Azure Front Door / Cloud CDN)
cues.why: Edge caching near users beats an in-region ElastiCache cluster for static, cacheable content.

cues.cue: Redis writes fail with OOM errors even though there are many keys
cues.pick: Switch to an allkeys-* policy (such as allkeys-lru) or add TTLs
cues.why: noeviction, or volatile-* with few TTL keys, leaves Redis nothing it is allowed to evict.

cues.cue: Small set of items is accessed constantly, while others see one-off scans
cues.pick: LFU (allkeys-lfu)
cues.why: LFU keeps frequently used keys even when a burst of one-time reads would push them out under LRU.

scenario.situation: An e-commerce company runs product pages on Amazon RDS for MySQL. Traffic is 95% reads, the same 5,000 products get most views, and prices may be up to a minute stale on product pages. The database is near its CPU limit, and management wants lower latency and cost. The caching layer must survive an Availability Zone failure without a cold start. Which solution best meets these requirements?
reasoning: DAX only fronts DynamoDB, so it is out because the database is RDS.
Adding more read replicas scales reads but keeps millisecond latency and adds cost, while the repeated reads of the same products point to a cache.
ElastiCache for Memcached has no replication or Multi-AZ failover, so a lost node means a cold cache. That fails the AZ requirement.
Write-behind is irrelevant to a read-heavy page and risks losing price updates. Cache-aside with a TTL fits data that can be a minute stale.
That leaves ElastiCache for Redis OSS/Valkey with replicas across AZs and automatic failover, using cache-aside, a TTL with jitter of about 60 seconds, and key deletion on price update.
scenario.answer: Use Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey or Redis OSS with Multi-AZ automatic failover, filled by cache-aside with a jittered TTL and deleted on update. It offloads the hot repeated reads at sub-millisecond latency and keeps a warm replica if an AZ fails.

memoryAids: ASIDE = App does the work; THROUGH = cache does the work; BEHIND = Buffered, may lose Bytes.
Memcached = Minimal and Multi-threaded; Redis/Valkey = Rich, Replicated, Retained (persisted).
volatile-* = 'only the mortal keys die': it evicts only keys with a TTL, so no TTLs means nothing can die and writes fail.
cheatSheet: Read-heavy, repeated queries on RDS/Aurora → ElastiCache with cache-aside and a TTL.
DynamoDB with microsecond reads and minimal code change → DAX, never ElastiCache.
Failover, persistence, backups, sorted sets or pub/sub in the question → Redis OSS/Valkey, not Memcached.
Money, orders or inventory writes → write-through or direct DB writes. Write-behind only when some loss is tolerable.
Update flow in cache-aside: write the database first, then delete the key. Never update the cached value in place.
Every cached key gets a TTL plus random jitter. The TTL is your safety net for missed invalidations.
Stampede → jitter + single-flight lock + early refresh. Penetration → cache nulls + Bloom filter. Hot key → local cache + key replication.
Set maxmemory-policy on purpose: allkeys-lru is the usual pure-cache choice, and allkeys-lfu suits a stable hot set.
Three stale-data paths in cache-aside: TTL not yet expired, a missed or failed delete, and a race where a slow reader writes an old value back after the delete.
Static global content → CDN (CloudFront, Azure Front Door, Cloud CDN), not an in-region cache.
Azure equivalent: Azure Cache for Redis. GCP equivalent: Memorystore (Redis/Valkey/Memcached). The same pattern logic applies.
The database stays the source of truth. If the cache is flushed, the system must be slower, not broken.
selfCheck: I can choose between ElastiCache, DAX, read replicas and a CDN from one line of scenario wording.
I can defend cache-aside with a TTL for a read-heavy workload, and write-through or write-behind for a write-heavy one, naming the data-loss trade-off.
I can explain why deleting a key beats updating it on write, and list three ways cache-aside still serves stale data.
I can tell stampede, hot key and penetration apart from their symptoms and give two fixes for each.
I can pick a Redis eviction policy and explain why a volatile-* policy causes OOM errors when keys lack TTLs.
I can justify Redis/Valkey vs Memcached using availability, persistence and data-type requirements.

objective.question: An e-commerce application runs on Amazon RDS for MySQL. About 90% of queries are repeated reads of product details, and the database CPU is high. The company wants to reduce read latency and database cost. Some staleness of a few minutes is acceptable. What should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Migrate the product table to Amazon DynamoDB and enable DAX
Add an Amazon SQS queue in front of the database to buffer reads
Increase the RDS instance size and enable Multi-AZ
Add Amazon ElastiCache and use a cache-aside pattern with a TTL on product keys
objective.explanation: Read-heavy RDS with a need to cut latency and cost is the classic trigger for ElastiCache with cache-aside and a TTL. DAX works only with DynamoDB. Multi-AZ is for availability, not read scaling. SQS buffers asynchronous work and cannot serve synchronous reads.

objective.question: A gaming company stores player profiles in Amazon DynamoDB. Reads must return in microseconds. The team wants the smallest possible change to existing application code. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
Amazon CloudFront in front of the DynamoDB endpoint
DynamoDB global tables
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with cache-aside logic in the application
objective.explanation: DAX is an in-memory, read-through/write-through cache for DynamoDB. It uses a DynamoDB-compatible API, so very little code changes, and it gives microsecond reads. ElastiCache needs custom cache logic. Global tables give multi-Region replication, not microsecond reads. CloudFront does not cache DynamoDB API calls.

objective.question: A company needs an in-memory cache for user sessions. The cache must survive the loss of a node, fail over automatically across Availability Zones, and support backups. Which option meets these needs?
options: Amazon ElastiCache with the Valkey or Redis OSS engine, with replicas and Multi-AZ enabled
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with Auto Discovery enabled
An in-process cache on each EC2 instance behind an Application Load Balancer
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached with several nodes
objective.explanation: Only the Valkey and Redis OSS engines in ElastiCache support replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, backups and persistence. Memcached has no replication or persistence, so the data on a lost node is gone. Auto Discovery only helps clients find nodes. Local in-process caches lose sessions when an instance is replaced.

objective.question: A team runs self-managed open-source Redis as a cache. When memory fills up, SET commands start failing with out-of-memory errors instead of old keys being removed. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The default maxmemory-policy is noeviction; set a policy such as allkeys-lru
Persistence is enabled; turn off AOF to free memory
The default policy is volatile-ttl; switch to volatile-random
Redis does not support eviction; switch to Memcached
objective.explanation: Open-source Redis defaults to noeviction, so writes fail when maxmemory is reached. For a pure cache, a policy such as allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu lets Redis evict keys. Redis does support eviction, volatile-ttl is not the default, and turning off persistence does not change eviction behaviour.

objective.question: An ElastiCache (Redis OSS) cluster uses the default parameter group. The application writes all keys without a TTL. Memory is now full and writes are failing. Why?
options: The default policy is volatile-lru, which only evicts keys that have a TTL, so no key is eligible for eviction
ElastiCache never evicts keys; you must scale out the cluster
Keys without a TTL are stored on disk and fill the volume
The default policy is allkeys-random, which cannot evict large keys
objective.explanation: The ElastiCache default parameter group uses volatile-lru. Volatile policies only consider keys with a TTL. If no key has a TTL, nothing can be evicted, and writes fail as they would under noeviction. The fix is to set TTLs or switch to an allkeys-* policy.

objective.question: A service uses cache-aside for product prices. When a price changes, which approach best avoids leaving a wrong value in the cache because of concurrent writers?
options: Update the database, then delete the cache key
Delete the cache key, then update the database, and never set a TTL
Update the database, then write the new value into the cache
Update the cache first, then update the database
objective.explanation: In cache-aside, write the database and then delete the key. Deletion is idempotent, so two writers cannot leave out-of-order values the way two concurrent SETs can. The next read reloads the fresh value. Updating the cache first risks caching a value the database never committed. You should still keep a TTL to bound any leftover staleness.

objective.question: Every day at exactly 00:00, a news site's database CPU spikes to 100% for a minute. Investigation shows that thousands of cache keys were all written at a nightly warm-up job with the same 24-hour TTL. What is the best fix?
options: Add random jitter (for example ±10%) to each key's TTL
Remove TTLs so keys never expire
Move from Redis to Memcached
Switch the eviction policy from LRU to LFU
objective.explanation: Keys that share one TTL expire together and cause a stampede of cache misses on the database. Jitter spreads the expiry times out. Changing the eviction policy does not affect TTL expiry. Removing TTLs causes unbounded staleness. Changing the engine does not fix synchronised expiry.

objective.question: A bot sends millions of requests for random product IDs that do not exist. Each request misses the cache and queries the database, which slows down. What is this problem called, and what is a suitable fix?
options: Cache stampede; add a mutex around cache refills
Cache eviction storm; switch to allkeys-lfu
Cache penetration; cache negative (not found) results with a short TTL or use a Bloom filter in front of the cache
Hot key; replicate the key to all shards
objective.explanation: Requests for keys that exist neither in the cache nor in the database are called cache penetration. Caching a short-lived 'not found' marker, or checking a Bloom filter of valid IDs first, stops these requests from reaching the database. Input validation and rate limiting also help. The other options solve different problems.

objective.question: During a flash sale, one product key receives so many reads that the single Redis shard holding it hits 100% CPU. Other shards are nearly idle. Which approach best relieves this hot key?
options: Lower the TTL of the key
Change the eviction policy to volatile-ttl
Use a short-lived local in-process cache on application servers and/or copy the key into several suffixed keys spread across shards or read replicas
Add more shards to the cluster
objective.explanation: A hot key lives in one hash slot, so adding shards does not spread its load. A small local cache absorbs most reads. Splitting the key into copies (for example product:42#1 to #N) spreads reads across shards or replicas. A lower TTL adds misses, and the eviction policy has no effect on read load.

objective.question: An IoT platform receives very high volumes of view-count and like-count updates. Losing a few seconds of counts during a rare cache failure is acceptable. The database is struggling with the write rate. Which caching pattern fits best?
options: Write-through
Read-through with a long TTL
Write-behind (write-back), batching updates from the cache to the database asynchronously
Cache-aside with delete-on-write
objective.explanation: Write-behind absorbs writes in the cache and flushes them to the database in batches. This cuts database write load, and the small risk of losing data is accepted here. Write-through still writes to the database on every update. Cache-aside and read-through mainly help reads.

objective.question: After a user edits their profile, the very next page load must show the new value. Reads are frequent. Which pattern best guarantees read-after-write freshness from the cache?
options: Write-behind with a 30-second flush interval
Memcached with no TTL
Write-through, so each write updates the database and the cache together, plus a TTL as a safety net
Cache-aside with a 10-minute TTL and no invalidation
objective.explanation: Write-through updates the cache as part of the write path, so the next read sees the new value. A TTL limits damage if a cache update ever fails. Cache-aside without invalidation can serve the old value until the TTL expires. Write-behind does not guarantee that the database is current.

objective.question: A Redis cache holds a small set of very popular keys. Every night, an analytics job reads millions of different keys once each. After the job, the cache hit ratio drops sharply for the popular keys. Which eviction policy would best protect the popular keys?
options: volatile-random
noeviction
allkeys-lfu
allkeys-lru
objective.explanation: Under LRU, a one-time scan makes millions of keys 'recently used' and pushes out the popular ones. LFU tracks how often keys are accessed, so keys read once by the scan stay cold and the popular keys survive. Random eviction can still remove hot keys, and noeviction causes write errors.

objective.question: A developer adds this Redis command before rebuilding an expensive cache entry after a miss. Other requests that fail to run the command wait briefly and then re-read the cache. What does this achieve?

code.code: SET lock:product:42 "worker-7f3a" NX PX 10000

options: It pins the key in memory so the eviction policy can never remove it
It replicates the key to 10,000 replicas to spread a hot key
It overwrites the product value and sets a 10,000-second TTL to stagger expiry
It creates a lock that only one client can acquire, which expires after 10 seconds, so only one request rebuilds the key and a stampede is avoided
objective.explanation: NX sets the key only if it does not exist, and PX 10000 gives it a 10,000 ms expiry, so it works as a short-lived mutex for cache rebuilds. PX is in milliseconds, not seconds, and SET does not affect eviction or replication.

objective.question: A mobile game needs a global leaderboard that shows each player's rank and the top 100 players in real time. Millions of score updates arrive per hour. The team wants a managed AWS service with the least custom code. Which solution should a solutions architect recommend?
options: Amazon ElastiCache (Redis OSS or Valkey) using sorted sets with ZADD and ZREVRANGE
Amazon RDS for MySQL with a read replica and ORDER BY score queries
Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of a table with a Scan on every request
Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached, storing each score as a separate key and sorting in the application
objective.explanation: Redis and Valkey sorted sets keep members ordered by score, so rank and top-N queries are fast server-side operations. Memcached has only simple key-value strings, and sorting on RDS or scanning through DAX would not scale to real-time ranking.

objective.question: An application reads a DynamoDB table through DAX. Updated items return fresh data when fetched with GetItem. However, Query results for the same partition sometimes show old values for several minutes after an update. What is the most likely cause?
options: The DAX cluster is evicting items with an LFU policy
DAX query cache results are not invalidated by writes, so they stay until their TTL expires
DynamoDB Query is always eventually consistent, and DAX cannot change this
DAX is configured as write-behind, so writes have not reached DynamoDB yet
objective.explanation: DAX has an item cache, which writes through DAX keep up to date, and a separate query cache. Writes do not invalidate the query cache, so cached Query and Scan results can stay stale until the query cache TTL expires. DAX is write-through to DynamoDB, not write-behind.

objective.question: A team uses write-through caching for a user-preferences service. Every write goes to both the database and Redis. After a few months, Redis memory is full of entries for users who have not logged in for a long time, and active users get evicted. What is the best fix?
options: Move the cache to Memcached, which never evicts data
Set a TTL on every entry and combine write-through with cache-aside lazy loading for misses
Disable the eviction policy so no entries are ever removed
Switch to write-behind so writes reach Redis faster
objective.explanation: Write-through caches every written item, even items that are never read again, so TTLs are needed to expire cold data. Cache-aside then reloads anything that expired. Write-behind does not solve cache churn, disabling eviction causes out-of-memory errors, and Memcached also evicts.

objective.question: A product service uses cache-aside with delete-on-update. Under load, the cache sometimes holds an old price indefinitely. The sequence is: Request A misses the cache and reads the old price from the database. Writer B updates the database and deletes the key. Request A then writes the old price into the cache. Which change most reliably limits the impact of this race?
options: Update the cache first and then the database
Remove the delete step and rely on the eviction policy
Increase the Redis instance size so the key is never evicted
Always set a TTL on cached entries, and optionally do a delayed second delete after the update
objective.explanation: A TTL bounds how long any stale value can survive, and a delayed second delete removes values written by in-flight readers. Updating the cache before the database adds new inconsistency, and eviction or instance size does nothing about correctness.

objective.question: What does this cache read function do differently from a plain TTL-based cache-aside read?

code.code:
import math, random, time

BETA = 1.0

def get(key):
    value, delta, expiry = cache.get_with_meta(key)
    now = time.time()
    if value is None or now - delta * BETA * math.log(random.random()) >= expiry:
        start = time.time()
        value = recompute(key)
        delta = time.time() - start
        cache.set(key, value, delta, ttl=TTL)
    return value

options: It randomly refreshes the key before it expires, with higher probability as expiry nears and when recompute is slow, to prevent a stampede
It spreads one hot key across several replicas by adding a random suffix
It caches a null value for keys that do not exist, to stop cache penetration
It locks the key so that only one process can ever read it
objective.explanation: This is probabilistic early expiration (XFetch). Because log(random()) is negative, the check sometimes triggers before expiry. The chance grows near expiry and with recompute time (delta), so one caller usually refreshes the value before a mass expiry. It does not lock, cache nulls or shard keys.

objective.question: To stop cache penetration, a team caches a 'NOT_FOUND' marker for missing product IDs with a 24-hour TTL. Now merchants complain that newly created products show as 'not found' for up to a day. What is the best fix?
options: Switch the eviction policy to allkeys-lfu so the markers are evicted first
Use a short TTL for negative entries and delete the marker when the product is created
Move from Redis to Memcached, which does not support negative caching
Stop caching misses entirely and add more database read replicas
objective.explanation: Negative cache entries need a much shorter TTL than normal entries, and the create path should invalidate the marker. Removing negative caching brings back penetration, eviction policy choice does not guarantee removal, and Memcached can store markers just like Redis.

objective.question: A team runs a self-managed Memcached pool of 4 nodes. The client picks a node with hash(key) % number_of_nodes. After a fifth node is added, the cache hit ratio falls close to zero and database load jumps, even though no keys expired. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Modulo hashing maps most keys to a different node when the node count changes. Use consistent hashing, for example a ketama-style client.
All keys had the same TTL and expired together. Add random jitter to the TTLs.
The new node has no LRU history, so it evicts keys from the other nodes. Disable LRU on the new node.
Memcached flushes every node when a new node joins the pool. Pre-warm the cache before adding nodes.
objective.explanation: With hash % N, changing N moves most keys to a new node, so nearly every lookup misses. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of the keys. Memcached does not flush peers or share LRU state, and the stem rules out expiry.

objective.question: In a cache-aside design, which write-path order is the safest default for updating a product?
options: Update the cache with the new value, then update the database.
Update the database, then overwrite the cache key with the new value.
Update the database, then delete the cache key, and keep a TTL on every key as a safety net.
Delete the cache key, then update the database.
objective.explanation: If you delete first, a concurrent reader can reload the old value before the database commit. If you write the cache first, the cache holds data the database may never commit. Overwriting after the update lets two writers leave the older value in the cache. Update the DB, then delete, with a TTL as a backstop.

objective.question: An ElastiCache (Redis OSS) node shows high latency and rising SwapUsage every night during the automatic backup. The custom parameter group sets reserved-memory-percent to 0. What is the most likely cause?
options: Backups switch the eviction policy to noeviction, so writes block until the snapshot finishes.
reserved-memory-percent controls the number of client connections, so new connections queue during the backup.
Backups always run on the primary and lock all keys, so latency is expected and cannot be reduced.

Backups use a forked process. Copy-on-write needs memory outside the dataset, and with no reserved memory the node swaps. Restore a reserved-memory value, such as the 25% default, or use a larger node.
objective.explanation: Snapshots fork the Redis process, and pages changed during the backup are copied. That memory must come from outside maxmemory. Setting reserved memory to 0 lets the dataset fill all RAM, which causes swapping. The other options describe behaviour Redis does not have.

objective.question: Whenever an admin updates a category, every Redis call from the application times out for several seconds. The cache holds tens of millions of keys. What is the problem in this invalidation code?
options: KEYS scans the whole keyspace in one blocking command, and Redis runs commands one at a time. Use SCAN in batches, or put a category version number in the key and increment it instead of deleting keys.
Redis cannot delete keys inside a loop. Wrap the loop in MULTI/EXEC.
The f-string pattern is not valid Redis glob syntax, so Redis retries the command.
DELETE is slow. Replace it with EXPIRE key 0.
objective.explanation: KEYS is O(N) over the entire keyspace and blocks all other commands while it runs. SCAN works in small steps. A versioned namespace such as product:v7:{cat_id}:… makes invalidation a single INCR, and old keys age out through their TTL. MULTI/EXEC would not fix the blocking scan.

objective.question: A retailer serves product images and a public catalog JSON from an origin in us-east-1. The responses are the same for every user. Users in Europe and India report slow page loads. Which change best reduces their latency?
options: Put Amazon CloudFront in front of the origin, with cache behaviours and TTLs for images and catalog JSON.
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) on the catalog table.
Add RDS read replicas in us-east-1.
Add an ElastiCache for Redis cluster in us-east-1 in front of the database.
objective.explanation: The latency comes from distance to one Region. Caching at edge locations fixes that. ElastiCache, read replicas and DAX all stay in us-east-1, so they reduce database load but not the network round trip for distant users.

objective.question: A team needs a cache for rendered HTML fragments. Requirements: plain string key-value only, a multithreaded engine that uses many cores on large nodes, scale out by adding nodes, no replication, no persistence and no backups. Losing a node's data is acceptable. Which option matches these requirements with the simplest design?
options: ElastiCache (Redis OSS) with cluster mode enabled, Multi-AZ and daily snapshots.
DynamoDB with DAX.
ElastiCache for Memcached with several nodes and Auto Discovery.
Amazon MemoryDB, for its durable multi-AZ transaction log.
objective.explanation: Memcached is a simple, multithreaded key-value cache that scales out across nodes and has no replication or persistence, which matches every requirement. MemoryDB and Multi-AZ Redis add durability and failover the team said it does not need. DAX caches DynamoDB items, not arbitrary HTML.

objective.question: An API Gateway REST API caches GET /orders?customerId=123 at the stage level. After caching was enabled, customers sometimes see another customer's orders. What is the most likely mistake?
options: The customerId query string (and the caller's identity) is not configured as a cache key, so all customers share one cached response. Add them as cache key parameters, or do not cache personalised responses.
API Gateway caches only POST requests by default, so GET responses come from Lambda warm containers.
Stage caching is eventually consistent across Availability Zones.
The cache TTL is too long. Reduce it to 30 seconds.
objective.explanation: API Gateway builds the cache key from the method parameters you mark as cache keys. If customerId is not included, every customer gets whichever response was cached first. A shorter TTL only narrows the window in which data leaks, and the other options are incorrect.

objective.question: An application on ElastiCache (Redis OSS) with cluster mode enabled runs the command below and gets an error. Which fix keeps the cluster sharded and lets the command work?

code.code:
> MGET user:42:profile user:42:settings
(error) CROSSSLOT Keys in request don't hash to the same slot

options: Rename the keys with a hash tag, such as {user:42}:profile and {user:42}:settings, so only the tag is hashed and both keys land in the same slot.
Add more shards so each key gets its own slot.
Wrap the MGET in MULTI/EXEC to make it cross-slot safe.
Disable cluster mode so all keys live on one shard.
objective.explanation: In Redis Cluster, multi-key commands need all keys in one hash slot. Hash tags make Redis hash only the part inside {}, so related keys stay together. Disabling cluster mode gives up scaling. More shards or MULTI/EXEC do not remove the slot rule.

objective.question: One Redis instance holds cache keys, all with TTLs, and background-job metadata with no TTL that must never be evicted. The team cannot split them into separate clusters this quarter. Which maxmemory-policy fits best?
options: noeviction
allkeys-random
volatile-lru
allkeys-lru
objective.explanation: volatile-lru evicts only keys that have an expiry, so the job keys with no TTL are protected and cache keys are still reclaimed. The allkeys-* policies can evict job data. noeviction makes writes fail when memory is full. Long term, separate the two workloads.

objective.question: A service writes a user's new address to the ElastiCache (Redis OSS) primary endpoint, then immediately reads it back through the reader endpoint. Sometimes the read returns the old address. What is the cause and the right fix?
options: The reader endpoint caches DNS for one hour. Lower the DNS TTL in the client.
Replicas apply writes only after a snapshot. Enable more frequent backups.
The key was evicted on the replica. Change the policy to noeviction.
Replication from primary to replicas is asynchronous. Read from the primary on read-after-write paths, and use replicas for reads that can tolerate lag.
objective.explanation: Redis replicas receive writes asynchronously, so there is a short lag window. Paths that need to see their own writes should read from the primary. DNS, eviction and snapshots do not explain a stale value on a replica.

objective.question: A team puts a Bloom filter of all valid product IDs in front of the cache to stop cache penetration. Which statement about this filter is correct?
options: It can say 'maybe present' for an ID that does not exist, but it never says 'absent' for an ID that was added.
A standard Bloom filter supports deleting IDs directly when products are removed.
It stores every product ID exactly, so its memory grows linearly with the ID length.
It can say an ID is absent when the ID actually exists, so some valid products will return 404.
objective.explanation: A Bloom filter has no false negatives and a tunable false-positive rate, so a few invalid IDs still reach the cache and database.
