selfCheck: I can finish any of the 12 designs in 45 minutes with requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram and three trade-offs, each with a stated decision.
I can name the AWS, Google Cloud and Azure managed service for cache, stream, queue, object storage, CDN and real-time push.
I can explain what happens in my design when a cache node, a shard or a downstream provider fails, including retries, DLQ and replication.
I can pick AP or CP for each component of a design and justify it in one sentence.
I can tell from an exam question's symptom (429s, hot key, slow uploads, write storm) which pattern fixes it and why the distractors do not.
I can compare token bucket vs sliding window, push vs pull fan-out, and geohash vs quadtree without notes.

objective.question: A new API is expected to handle 50 million requests per day. You plan peak capacity at about 3x the average. Roughly what peak QPS should you design for?
options: About 1,500–1,800 QPS
About 50,000 QPS
About 15,000 QPS
About 150 QPS
objective.explanation: 50 million divided by about 10^5 seconds per day gives roughly 500–580 QPS on average, so 3x is about 1,500–1,800 QPS. 150 QPS is too low, and 15,000 or 50,000 QPS are off by an order of magnitude or more.

objective.question: A URL shortener must create 100 million new short codes per day and must not run out of codes for several decades. Using Base62 encoding, what is the shortest code length that meets this goal?
options: 6 characters
10 characters
7 characters
5 characters
objective.explanation: 62^7 is about 3.5 trillion keys, which lasts about 35,000 days (roughly 95 years) at 100M/day. 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, which lasts only about 1.5 years, and 5 characters is far smaller. 10 characters works but is longer than needed.

objective.question: The marketing team of a URL shortener needs every click counted, including repeat clicks from the same browser. Which redirect response should the service return?
options: 302 Found (temporary redirect)
308 Permanent Redirect
404 Not Found with a link in the body
301 Moved Permanently
objective.explanation: A 302 is not cached by browsers by default, so every click reaches your servers and can be logged. 301 and 308 are permanent redirects that browsers cache, so repeat clicks skip your servers. A 404 breaks the redirect.

objective.question: A public API must enforce an average limit of 100 requests per minute per user. It should still allow short bursts, and the limiter must use little memory per user. Which algorithm fits best?
options: Sliding window log
Leaking bucket with a fixed outflow rate
Token bucket
Fixed window counter
objective.explanation: A token bucket stores only a token count and a timestamp per user. It allows bursts up to the bucket size while enforcing the refill rate on average. A fixed window allows up to 2x traffic at window edges. A sliding window log stores every timestamp, which uses a lot of memory. A leaking bucket smooths traffic and does not allow bursts.

objective.question: A search box must show the top 5 suggestions within about 100 ms as the user types each character. Query volume is very high. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Use a trie where each node stores the precomputed top-k completions, rebuild it offline from query logs, and serve it from memory or cache
Run a full-text search across all documents on every keystroke and rank the results live
Store each full query in a key-value store keyed by a hash of the complete query
Run SQL LIKE 'prefix%' on the raw query log table on every keystroke
objective.explanation: Storing top-k at each trie node makes a lookup a simple walk down the prefix with no ranking at request time. Rebuilding offline keeps the read path fast and cacheable. A LIKE scan on the log and live full-text ranking are too slow at scale, and hashing complete queries cannot answer prefix lookups.

objective.question: In a social news feed, most users have a few hundred followers, but some celebrities have 50 million. Posts must appear quickly, and home-feed reads must stay fast. Which approach is the standard choice?
options: Pure fan-out on read for every user
Send every post to every user's mailbox using a single global queue
A hybrid: fan-out on write for normal users, and merge celebrity posts in at read time
Pure fan-out on write for every user, including celebrities
objective.explanation: Fan-out on write gives fast reads, but writing one celebrity post into 50 million feeds is very costly. A hybrid pre-computes feeds for normal authors and pulls celebrity posts in at read time. Pure fan-out on read makes every feed load slow, and a single global queue does not scale.

objective.question: You are designing a WhatsApp-style chat. Messages must reach online users in near real time, and offline users must get them later. What is the best delivery design?
options: Messages are sent by email (SMTP) and the app reads the inbox
Messages are kept only in chat server memory and dropped if the recipient is offline
Clients keep persistent WebSocket connections to chat servers; messages are stored durably, and offline users get them on reconnect plus a push notification
Clients poll a REST endpoint every second for new messages
objective.explanation: WebSockets give low-latency, two-way delivery over one long-lived connection. Durable storage with sync on reconnect and push notifications covers offline users. Short polling wastes resources and adds latency, SMTP is not suitable, and memory-only storage loses messages.

objective.question: A pastebin service stores paste metadata in Amazon DynamoDB. Some users paste content up to 5 MB. How should you store the paste content?
options: Store the content in Amazon S3, and keep the S3 object key plus metadata in DynamoDB
Compress the paste and store it as a DynamoDB attribute in every case
Split each paste across many DynamoDB items in the same table
Store the content in the DynamoDB item, because DynamoDB has no item size limit
objective.explanation: DynamoDB items have a 400 KB maximum size, so large blobs belong in S3 with a pointer in the database. Splitting a paste across items adds complexity for no benefit. Compression does not guarantee that a 5 MB paste fits under 400 KB.

objective.question: Creators upload videos of up to 20 GB to a YouTube-like platform. Viewers on slow and fast networks must get smooth playback. Which pipeline is correct?
options: Store videos in DynamoDB items, and serve them directly from the database
Upload to S3, then serve only the original file through the CDN
Use S3 multipart upload; an upload event puts a job on a queue; workers transcode into several resolutions and bitrates, segmented for adaptive streaming (HLS/DASH); deliver through a CDN
Upload with a single PUT request to the web server, store the file on the server disk, and stream the original file
objective.explanation: Multipart upload handles large files reliably and allows retries per part. Queue-driven transcoding into multiple renditions enables adaptive bitrate streaming, and a CDN serves video close to viewers. A single PUT to a web server does not scale, DynamoDB cannot hold video, and serving only the original file fails on slow networks.

objective.question: A ride-hailing app indexes driver locations by geohash. A rider requests a car, and the system searches only the rider's own geohash cell. Drivers just across the cell boundary are never matched. What is the correct fix?
options: Search the rider's cell and its 8 neighbouring cells, then filter results by actual distance
Store all drivers in one list and compute the distance to every driver
Index drivers by latitude only, using a B-tree
Use a longer geohash so that cells are smaller
objective.explanation: Points that are close together can sit in different cells with different geohash prefixes, so you must also query the 8 neighbours and then filter by true distance. Longer geohashes make the edge problem worse. A latitude-only index and a full scan are both inefficient.

objective.question: A distributed cache has 10 nodes. You add an 11th node. Which statement about consistent hashing is correct?
options: Only about 1/11 of the keys move, and virtual nodes help spread the load evenly
Exactly half of the keys move to the new node
No keys move until the cluster restarts
Almost all keys move, just as with hash(key) mod N
objective.explanation: Consistent hashing remaps only about K/N keys when a node joins or leaves. Virtual nodes give each physical node many positions on the ring, which fixes uneven load. Modulo hashing is the approach that remaps most keys.

objective.question: A key-value store keeps N=3 replicas of each key. The team wants reads to overlap with the latest acknowledged write. Both reads and writes must still succeed if one replica is down. Which setting should they use?
objective.explanation: W=2, R=2 gives R+W=4 > 3, so read and write sets always overlap. Each operation still needs only 2 of 3 nodes, so one node can fail. W=3 blocks writes when any node is down, and W=1 with R=1 or R=2 gives R+W ≤ 3, so there is no guaranteed overlap.

objective.question: A URL shortener uses a Snowflake-style 64-bit ID generator with the bit layout shown. Ignoring clock limits, what is the maximum number of unique IDs one worker can generate per second?

code.code:
| 1 bit sign | 41 bits ms timestamp | 10 bits worker ID | 12 bits sequence |

id = (timestamp_ms - EPOCH) << 22 | (worker_id << 12) | sequence

objective.explanation: The 12-bit sequence gives 4,096 IDs per millisecond, and there are 1,000 ms in a second, so the limit is 4,096,000 per second per worker. 1,024 is the number of workers that 10 bits allow, not a per-second limit.

objective.question: A team implements a 100 requests-per-minute limit with the Redis logic below. Users report that some clients get far more than 100 requests through in a short time. What is the cause?
options: The EXPIRE call deletes the key too early, so the counter always starts at zero
Redis keys with a TTL are evicted first under memory pressure, so the counter is lost on every request
Fixed windows reset at the minute boundary, so a client can send 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00
INCR is not atomic, so concurrent requests from the same user lose updates
objective.explanation: This is a fixed window counter, and it allows up to twice the limit across a window boundary. INCR is atomic in Redis, and the TTL logic is correct. A sliding window counter or a token bucket removes the boundary burst.

objective.question: A web crawler uses a Bloom filter to track URLs it has already seen across billions of URLs. Which statement about this design is correct?
options: The filter gives exact answers, but it needs memory proportional to the total URL length
The filter supports deleting URLs, so recrawl scheduling can remove entries when pages change
The filter may wrongly say a seen URL is new, so some pages are crawled twice, but it never skips a page
The filter may wrongly say a new URL was seen, so a few pages are skipped, but it never says a seen URL is new
objective.explanation: Bloom filters have false positives but no false negatives. For a crawler, this means a small fraction of new URLs is wrongly skipped and no URL is fetched twice. A standard Bloom filter cannot delete entries, and its memory depends on the target error rate, not on URL length.

objective.question: A notification service reads jobs from Amazon SQS standard queues and calls a push provider. During a provider slowdown, workers time out and retry, and many users receive the same push notification two or three times. Which change fixes this most reliably?
options: Increase the SQS visibility timeout to 12 hours
Send each notification from two workers in parallel and keep the first response
Attach an idempotency key to each notification and have workers record sent keys in a fast store such as DynamoDB or Redis, skipping keys already sent
Switch to an SQS FIFO queue and remove all retries
objective.explanation: SQS standard queues deliver at least once, and retries after timeouts also cause duplicates, so the consumer must be idempotent. A dedup check on an idempotency key handles both cases. Removing retries loses notifications. A very long visibility timeout delays recovery and still does not stop duplicates from provider-side timeouts.

objective.question: A distributed cache uses consistent hashing with 4 physical nodes, each placed once on the ring. Monitoring shows one node holds about 45% of the keys while another holds about 10%. What is the standard fix?
options: Give each physical node many virtual nodes on the ring
Replicate every key to all 4 nodes
Increase the hash output from 32 bits to 128 bits
Switch to modulo hashing (hash(key) % 4) so keys spread evenly
objective.explanation: With only a few points on the ring, the gaps between nodes are uneven, so the load is uneven. Virtual nodes place each server at many points on the ring, which evens out the load and spreads keys more evenly when a node leaves. Modulo hashing remaps most keys on every resize. A larger hash range does not change how unevenly the few nodes are placed.

objective.question: A product page caches a very popular item in Amazon ElastiCache with a 5-minute TTL. Every time the key expires, database CPU spikes to 100% for a few seconds. Which approach best addresses this?
options: Use request coalescing: let one request take a short lock and rebuild the value while others serve the stale copy or wait, and add jitter to TTLs
Add more read replicas until the spike disappears
Lower the TTL to 30 seconds so each rebuild is smaller
Remove the TTL so the item is never refreshed
objective.explanation: This is a cache stampede: many requests miss at the same moment and all hit the database. A single rebuilder (lock, or a single-flight pattern) plus serving stale data and TTL jitter stops the stampede. A shorter TTL makes stampedes happen more often, and replicas only add cost without fixing the cause.

objective.question: A chat app stores messages in Amazon DynamoDB. The most common query is to load the latest 50 messages of a conversation in order, then page backward. Which key design fits best?
options: Partition key: sender_user_id; sort key: timestamp; Query both users and merge on the client
Partition key: date; sort key: conversation_id#timestamp
Partition key: conversation_id; sort key: a time-sortable message_id; Query with ScanIndexForward=false and Limit=50
Partition key: message_id; GSI on conversation_id; Scan with a filter
objective.explanation: Grouping messages by conversation_id and sorting by a time-ordered ID lets one Query return the newest 50 messages. LastEvaluatedKey then gives cheap backward paging. Scans are expensive and slow. Keying by date puts all of a day's traffic on one partition, which creates a hot partition.

objective.question: Put these steps of a web crawler's main fetch loop in the correct order: (A) parse the page and extract links, (B) take a URL from the frontier's per-host queue, (C) check the host's robots.txt rules, (D) normalise extracted URLs and drop ones already seen, (E) resolve DNS and fetch the page, (F) check the content fingerprint for duplicate pages, (G) add the new URLs to the frontier.
options: B → E → C → A → F → D → G
C → B → E → A → D → F → G
B → C → E → A → D → G → F
B → C → E → F → A → D → G
objective.explanation: You must check robots.txt before fetching. You also check the content fingerprint before spending work on parsing a duplicate page. Link normalisation and URL dedupe come after extraction and before enqueueing. The other orders either fetch before checking robots.txt or run content dedupe after the links are already queued.

objective.question: An API uses the rate limiter below against Amazon ElastiCache for Redis. During a 30-second primary failover, every API call returns HTTP 429 and the whole product goes down. What is the root cause and the best fix?
options: The limiter fails closed; on Redis errors it should fail open, ideally with a coarse local per-server limit as a fallback
ElastiCache does not support INCR during failover, so you must use DynamoDB instead
EXPIRE is not atomic with INCR, so keys never expire during failover
The fixed window is too short; switch to a sliding-window log
objective.explanation: The except branch returns False, so a limiter outage blocks all traffic. For most APIs the limiter is a protection layer, so failing open with a local fallback limit keeps the product up. The other options describe real details, but none of them explains why every request was rejected.

objective.question: A URL shortener stores mappings in Amazon DynamoDB with short_code as the partition key. Users can choose a custom alias. Two users submitted the same alias within milliseconds, and both got a success response. Which fix guarantees uniqueness?
options: Use PutItem with a condition expression attribute_not_exists(short_code) and return a conflict error if the condition fails
Enable DynamoDB Streams and delete the later duplicate when it is detected
Add a random suffix to every custom alias
Do a strongly consistent GetItem first and call PutItem only if the item is absent
objective.explanation: A conditional write is atomic, so only one writer can create the item. Read-then-write still has a race window between the read and the write. Streams only clean up after the damage is done, and a random suffix breaks the custom-alias requirement.

objective.question: In a group chat, users sometimes see replies appear above the messages they answer. Messages are sorted by the sent_at timestamp that the sender's phone supplies. What is the correct fix?
options: Assign each message a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation on the server side, and sort by that number
Sort messages by their random UUID
Send all messages from all conversations through a single SQS FIFO queue
Run NTP on all chat servers
objective.explanation: Phone clocks drift and can be set wrong, so client timestamps cannot give a reliable order. A server-assigned, per-conversation sequence gives one agreed order. Server NTP does not fix client clocks, UUIDs carry no order, and one global FIFO queue becomes a throughput bottleneck.

objective.question: Drivers send their location every 4 seconds to the table below. In a large city such as Bengaluru, writes are throttled at peak hours, while smaller cities have no problems. What is the mistake?

code.code:
Table: DriverLocations (Amazon DynamoDB)
Partition key: city_id
Sort key:      driver_id
Attributes:    lat, lng, geohash, status, updated_at
Write pattern: every active driver, every 4 s

options: Using city_id as the partition key puts all of a big city's writes on one hot key; partition by a finer key such as a geohash prefix, or keep live locations in an in-memory geo index
DynamoDB cannot store latitude and longitude
Drivers should send their location every 30 seconds
The sort key should be updated_at instead of driver_id
objective.explanation: A low-cardinality partition key concentrates heavy write traffic on one partition and hits per-partition throughput limits. A finer spatial key, or an in-memory store such as Redis GEO for the live positions, spreads the load. Changing the sort key does not spread writes, and sending updates less often hurts matching accuracy.

objective.question: A video platform serves HLS segments through Amazon CloudFront. Each player appends ?token=<per-user JWT> to every segment URL for authorisation. The cache policy includes all query strings in the cache key. Viewers buffer often, and the cache hit ratio is under 5%. What is the cause?
options: Each viewer's unique token creates a unique cache key, so almost every request misses and goes to the origin
CloudFront cannot cache .ts or .m4s files
The origin S3 bucket is in a different region from the viewers
The segment duration is too short
objective.explanation: Including a per-user token in the cache key makes every URL unique, which defeats the CDN. The fix is to remove the token from the cache key and validate it at the edge, or to use signed cookies. The other options do not explain a near-zero hit ratio.

objective.question: An autocomplete service rebuilds its top-k prefix tables once a week from search logs. During a breaking news event, a trending query does not appear in the suggestions for days. What is the best fix?
options: Query the search-log database directly on every keystroke
Increase the maximum depth of the trie
Add a streaming layer that counts recent queries over short time windows, and merge those counts with the batch top-k at serving time
Lower the cache TTL on suggestion responses
objective.explanation: The data is stale because of the weekly batch, not because of caching. A real-time layer for recent counts, merged with the batch results, surfaces trends within minutes. A shorter TTL still serves the same old tables, and querying the log database on every keystroke cannot meet the latency target.

objective.question: A Dynamo-style key-value store uses N=3 replicas. Some keys are written once and then rarely read. Over months, replicas of these keys drift apart after node outages. Which mechanism finds and repairs this divergence efficiently?
options: Hinted handoff
Vector clocks
Background anti-entropy that compares Merkle trees between replicas
Read repair
objective.explanation: Merkle trees let replicas compare hashes of key ranges and sync only the ranges that differ, so even keys that are never read get repaired. Read repair only fixes keys that are read. Hinted handoff only covers temporary outages, and hints can be lost. Vector clocks detect conflicting versions but do not find which replicas differ.

objective.question: A notification worker sends push messages from Amazon SQS. Its dead-letter queue grows by thousands of messages a day. All of them failed five times with the provider error 'unregistered device token'. What is the right change?
options: Add more workers
Move to an SQS FIFO queue
Treat this error as permanent: do not retry, and remove or deactivate the token in the device registry
Increase maxReceiveCount to 20
objective.explanation: An unregistered token will never succeed, so retrying wastes capacity and fills the DLQ. You should classify errors: retry transient ones with backoff, and act immediately on permanent ones. More retries or more workers only make the waste worse.

objective.question: Users of a news feed see the same post twice when they scroll down while new posts are arriving. What is the mistake in this API, and what is the fix?

code.code:
-- GET /v1/feed?page=3&size=20
SELECT post_id, author_id, created_at
FROM feed_items
WHERE user_id = :uid
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40;

options: The page size is too small
An index on user_id alone will fix it
ORDER BY should be ascending
Offset pagination shifts when new rows are inserted at the top; use cursor (keyset) pagination based on the last seen created_at and post_id
objective.explanation: New posts push older rows down, so OFFSET 40 returns rows the user already saw. A cursor such as WHERE (created_at, post_id) < (:last_ts, :last_id) stays stable and is also faster on deep pages. Page size, sort direction and indexing do not fix the shifting.

objective.question: In a ride-hailing system, which operation needs strong consistency rather than eventual consistency?
options: Deducting the fare from the rider's wallet balance
The total trip count shown on a driver's profile
A rider's 'last seen online' status
The like count on a driver's rating comment
objective.explanation: A wallet deduction must never double-charge or overdraw, so it needs strong consistency and idempotent transactions. Like counts, presence and profile counters can be stale for a few seconds with no real harm.

objective.question: A crawler runs 1,000 fetch workers, but throughput is far below target. CPU and network bandwidth are both low. Profiling shows most worker time is spent waiting on hostname resolution. What is the best fix?
options: Run a local caching DNS resolver for the crawler fleet and resolve hostnames ahead of time for URLs waiting in the frontier
Increase the size of the Bloom filter
Move to larger instances
Double the number of fetch workers
objective.explanation: DNS lookups are slow and repeated, so they are a classic crawler bottleneck. A local cache with early resolution removes most of that waiting. More workers or bigger machines just add more waiting threads, and the Bloom filter has nothing to do with DNS.

objective.question: Product prices use cache-aside reads with a 24-hour TTL. Sometimes the cache shows an old price for hours after an update. Which change fixes the write path below?
options: Keep the order but wrap both calls in a try/except
Switch to write-behind caching so the database is updated later
Update the database first, then delete the cache key so the next read reloads it, and keep a shorter TTL as a safety net
Increase the TTL to 7 days so the cache is hit more often
objective.explanation: Writing the cache first leaves wrong data if the DB update fails. Concurrent writers and readers can also put a stale value back into the cache. Updating the DB and then invalidating the key, with a short TTL as a backstop, removes most of these races. Write-behind adds a risk of data loss.

subjective.question: Compare three ways to generate short codes for a URL shortener: hashing the long URL, a global counter encoded in Base62, and a distributed ID generator. Which would you choose and why?
subjective.answer: Hashing the long URL (for example MD5, then taking the first 7 characters) needs no coordination, but collisions happen. You must check the database and retry, and the same URL always maps to the same code, which may or may not be what you want. A global counter encoded in Base62 never collides and gives short codes. However, one counter is a single point of failure, and sequential codes are guessable. A distributed generator removes the bottleneck. You can give each server a pre-allocated range of IDs from a ticket service, or use a Snowflake-style ID made of timestamp, machine ID and sequence. Each server then allocates locally, and the ID is still unique. I would choose range allocation plus Base62. ID allocation must be consistent (CP), but a server only contacts the coordinator when its range runs out. If guessability matters, I would shuffle the bits or add a random suffix.
keyPoints: Hashing gives collisions, so you need check-and-retry logic
A counter in Base62 avoids collisions but is a single point of failure and is guessable
Range allocation or Snowflake-style IDs remove the bottleneck
Unique ID allocation needs consistency (CP)

subjective.question: Do a back-of-envelope estimate for a URL shortener with 100 million new URLs per day, a 10:1 read-to-write ratio, 5 years of retention, and about 500 bytes per record.
subjective.answer: Writes: 100M per day divided by about 10^5 seconds is about 1,000 to 1,200 QPS on average. At 2–3x for peak, that is about 3,000 QPS. Reads are 10x writes, so about 12,000 QPS on average and 30,000 or more at peak. Storage: 100M per day times 365 times 5 is about 180 billion records. At 500 bytes each, that is about 90 TB before replication, or about 270 TB with 3 replicas. Key space: 7 Base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes, which is plenty. These numbers drive the design. The system is read-heavy, so I put a cache such as Redis in front of the database and use a CDN or edge caching for popular links. A few hot URLs take most of the traffic, so caching the top 20% of daily reads covers most requests. 90 TB needs a partitioned key-value store, sharded by short code.
keyPoints: About 1,200 write QPS on average, about 3,000 at peak
About 12,000 read QPS on average because of the 10:1 ratio
About 90 TB raw over 5 years, multiplied by the replication factor
Read-heavy, so add a cache and CDN, and shard by short code

subjective.question: Design a distributed rate limiter for an API served by 50 stateless servers. Cover the algorithm, storage, failure handling and client response.
subjective.answer: I would use a token bucket per user or API key. It allows bursts and keeps only a token count and a timestamp. The state must be shared, because a user's requests hit any of the 50 servers. I keep it in a central in-memory store such as Redis. The check-and-decrement must be atomic, using a Lua script or atomic increment with expiry, to avoid race conditions. The limiter can run in the API gateway or as middleware. Rules (limits per endpoint and tier) live in config and are cached locally. When a request is over the limit, I return HTTP 429 Too Many Requests with headers for the limit, the remaining requests and Retry-After. If Redis is unavailable, I choose between fail-open (allow traffic, which protects availability) and fail-closed (block traffic, which protects the backend). Most public APIs fail open. For very high scale, servers can keep local counters and sync them in batches, accepting small inaccuracy.
keyPoints: Token bucket per key; shared state in a central store such as Redis
Atomic operations (Lua or INCR with expiry) to avoid races
HTTP 429 with limit, remaining and Retry-After headers
Decide on fail-open vs fail-closed; local counters trade accuracy for latency

subjective.question: Explain fan-out on write vs fan-out on read for a news feed, and when you would use each.
subjective.answer: Fan-out on write (push) copies a new post ID into every follower's pre-computed feed, usually a list in a cache. Reads are then very fast, because the feed is ready. The cost is heavy write amplification: one post by a user with 50 million followers means 50 million writes. It also wastes work for inactive users. Fan-out on read (pull) stores posts only on the author's timeline. When a user opens the feed, the system fetches recent posts from everyone they follow and merges them. Writes are cheap, but reads are slow and expensive, and feeds are read far more often than posts are written. Most real systems use a hybrid. Normal users' posts are pushed, while celebrity posts are pulled and merged at read time. Inactive users may be skipped during push. The feed favours availability (AP). A post appearing a few seconds late is acceptable, so asynchronous queues handle the fan-out.
keyPoints: Push gives fast reads but high write amplification
Pull gives cheap writes but slow, costly reads
Hybrid: push for normal users, pull for celebrities
Feeds are AP, and async queues do the fan-out

subjective.question: Design the message flow for a WhatsApp-style one-to-one chat. Cover connections, storage, ordering and delivery receipts.
subjective.answer: Each client keeps a persistent WebSocket to a chat server. A presence and session service records which server each user is connected to. When A sends a message, A's server assigns a message ID that is ordered within the conversation, for example a per-chat sequence number or a time-based ID. It writes the message durably to a write-optimised store, partitioned by conversation ID, such as a wide-column or log-structured store. It then sends an acknowledgement back to A, which is the 'sent' tick. Next it looks up B's server and forwards the message through a queue or pub/sub. If B is online, B's client acknowledges, which gives the 'delivered' tick. If B is offline, the message waits in storage and a push notification goes out. B syncs from its last seen sequence number on reconnect. Clients deduplicate by message ID, because retries happen. Chat is write-heavy, so we partition and use queues. Chat history favours availability (AP), and ordering only needs to hold within a conversation, not globally.
keyPoints: Persistent WebSockets plus a session/presence service
Persist before acknowledging; partition by conversation ID
Per-conversation ordering with sequence IDs; clients dedupe on retry
Offline users: push notification plus sync from last sequence number

subjective.question: Design a notification system that sends push, SMS and email notifications for many internal services.
subjective.answer: Internal services call one notification API with a user ID, template, channel preferences and priority. The API validates the request, checks the user's preferences and opt-outs, applies rate limits so users are not spammed, and fills the template. It then publishes to a separate queue for each channel: push, SMS and email. Separate queues mean a slow SMS provider does not block push. Worker pools consume each queue and call third-party providers, such as the Apple and Google push services, an SMS gateway and an email service. Failures are retried with exponential backoff, and messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue. Each notification has an idempotency key so retries do not send duplicates. Delivery is at-least-once, so deduplication matters. A notification log stores status for tracking and analytics. Device tokens and contact details live in a user store. Trade-offs include at-least-once vs exactly-once delivery, and high-priority queues for OTPs vs batching for marketing messages.
keyPoints: Single API that checks preferences, opt-outs and rate limits
A separate queue and worker pool per channel
Retries with backoff, a dead-letter queue and idempotency keys
Priority separation: OTPs vs bulk marketing

subjective.question: Walk through the video upload and playback pipeline of a YouTube-like service on AWS.
subjective.answer: The client asks the API for upload permission and gets pre-signed URLs. It then uploads directly to Amazon S3 using multipart upload, which suits large files: parts upload in parallel and failed parts can be retried. S3 objects can be up to 5 TB. When the upload completes, an event places a job on a queue. Transcoding workers split the video and encode several resolutions and bitrates, for example 240p to 4K. They package the output into short segments with manifests for HLS or DASH, and generate thumbnails. Outputs are stored in S3. Video metadata such as title, owner, status and S3 keys goes into a database. The player downloads the manifest and fetches segments through a CDN such as Amazon CloudFront. Adaptive bitrate switching picks a quality that matches the viewer's bandwidth. Trade-offs include pre-transcoding all renditions vs transcoding unpopular videos on demand, how much to cache at the edge vs storage cost, and moving rarely watched videos to cheaper storage classes.
keyPoints: Pre-signed URLs and S3 multipart upload; the API servers never carry the bytes
Queue-driven transcoding into multiple renditions and segments
HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate delivered via CDN
Metadata in a DB; blobs in S3; storage tiering for the long tail

subjective.question: How would you store and query driver locations in a ride-hailing system, and how do you avoid assigning one driver to two riders?
subjective.answer: Drivers send their location every few seconds, which is a write-heavy stream. I would not write each update to a relational database. Instead, a location service keeps the current position in memory, for example in Redis geospatial sets or an in-memory index, partitioned by city or region. The index uses geohash or a quadtree. To find nearby drivers, I query the rider's cell and its neighbouring cells, then filter and rank by real distance or ETA. Location history goes to a log or stream for analytics. Assignment is different. It needs consistency (CP). When the matching service offers a trip to a driver, it must atomically change the driver's status from available to reserved. It uses a conditional write, compare-and-set, or a short lease on the driver record. If the driver declines or the lease times out, the status goes back to available. This prevents double booking even when two matchers pick the same driver at once.
keyPoints: Location updates are write-heavy: in-memory, partitioned by region
Geohash or quadtree; query neighbouring cells, then filter by distance or ETA
Trip assignment is CP: atomic conditional update or lease on driver status
Location history streamed to a log for analytics

subjective.question: Design search autocomplete that returns the top 5 suggestions per prefix with low latency.
subjective.answer: I would split the system into a read path and a build path. The build path collects search query logs. A batch or streaming job aggregates the logs, for example daily or hourly, into query frequencies. It can also weight recent queries more heavily and filter out offensive terms. From this it builds a trie, and at each node it precomputes and stores the top-k completions for that prefix. The trie is serialised, sharded by prefix range, and loaded into in-memory servers. A prefix-to-suggestions map in a cache also works. The read path is then just a lookup with no ranking at request time. Responses are cacheable at the CDN and in the browser, because the same prefixes repeat. Clients reduce load by debouncing keystrokes and only sending requests after 1–2 characters. Trade-offs: freshness vs cost (rebuilding often vs rarely), memory use of storing top-k at every node, and sharding by prefix, where popular letters need finer splits to avoid hot shards.
keyPoints: Offline aggregation of query logs into frequencies
Trie with precomputed top-k at each node, held in memory
Cache at the CDN and browser; client debounce
Trade-offs: freshness, memory, hot prefix shards

subjective.question: Design a distributed key-value store. Explain partitioning, replication, quorum and conflict handling.
subjective.answer: Partitioning uses consistent hashing. Keys and nodes sit on a hash ring, and each key belongs to the next node clockwise. When a node joins or leaves, only about K/N keys move. Virtual nodes give each server many positions on the ring, which balances load and lets bigger machines take more. Replication copies each key to the next N distinct nodes, for example N=3, ideally across availability zones. Quorum: a write succeeds after W acknowledgements and a read queries R replicas. With R + W > N, such as N=3, W=2, R=2, read and write sets overlap, so a read sees the latest write while one node can be down. Lower W or R gives lower latency and higher availability, but reads may be stale. Conflicts from concurrent writes are resolved with last-write-wins timestamps (simple, but can lose data) or with vector clocks that keep conflicting versions for the client to merge. Repair uses read repair, hinted handoff and background anti-entropy with Merkle trees.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; about K/N keys move
Replication factor N across failure domains
R + W > N for overlap; N=3, W=2, R=2 is common
Conflicts: LWW vs vector clocks; read repair, hinted handoff, Merkle trees

subjective.question: Design a web crawler that fetches a billion pages a month politely and without duplicates.
subjective.answer: A billion pages a month is about 400 pages per second on average, and more at peak. That makes this a write-heavy, queue-driven system. It starts from seed URLs placed in a URL frontier. The frontier has priority queues (based on importance and how often a page changes) and per-host queues. Each host is handled by one worker at a time, with a delay between requests, so we stay polite. Workers check robots.txt (cached per host), resolve DNS through a local cache, and fetch pages. Content goes to blob storage such as S3, with metadata in a database. A content fingerprint, such as a hash, detects duplicate pages. The parser extracts links and normalises them. A URL-seen check, often a Bloom filter backed by a store, drops URLs already crawled. Then new links go back to the frontier. Workers are partitioned by host hash. Trade-offs: a Bloom filter saves memory but has false positives, which means a few pages are skipped. Other trade-offs are crawl freshness vs breadth, and defending against spider traps with depth limits.
keyPoints: About 400 pages/second; queue-driven and partitioned by host
URL frontier with priority and per-host politeness queues
robots.txt, DNS caching, depth limits against traps
Dedup: Bloom filter for URLs, content hash for pages

subjective.question: How do you structure a 45-minute system design interview, and how do you decide between consistency and availability for different designs?
subjective.answer: I spend about 5 minutes on requirements: functional, non-functional and scale. I agree on scope before drawing anything. I spend about 5 minutes on estimates: QPS (1 day is about 10^5 seconds, and peak is 2–3x average), storage and read/write ratio. Next comes about 5 minutes on the API and the data model. Then about 15 minutes on the high-level diagram, and about 10 minutes on a deep dive into the hardest part. I keep the last minutes for three explicit trade-offs and for failure cases. For CAP, I decide per feature, not per system. Feeds, chat history, caches and view counts favour availability (AP), because slightly stale data is fine. Payments, trip assignment, inventory and unique ID allocation need consistency (CP), because a double charge or double booking is unacceptable. I also state the read/write profile. Read-heavy designs get caches and a CDN. Write-heavy designs get partitioning, queues and log-structured stores.
keyPoints: Requirements, estimates, API, data model, diagram, deep dive, trade-offs
Use 10^5 seconds per day and 2–3x for peak in estimates
Choose CAP per feature: AP for feeds and caches, CP for payments and IDs
Read-heavy: cache plus CDN; write-heavy: partitioning plus queues

subjective.question: Explain what this Redis Lua script does, why it is written as a Lua script rather than separate commands, and how you would call it from 50 API servers.

code.code:
local tokens = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 't') or ARGV[1])
local last = tonumber(redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'ts') or ARGV[3])
local cap, rate, now = tonumber(ARGV[1]), tonumber(ARGV[2]), tonumber(ARGV[3])
tokens = math.min(cap, tokens + (now - last) * rate)
local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then tokens = tokens - 1; allowed = 1 end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 120)
return allowed

subjective.answer: This is a token bucket. For each user key, it reads the current tokens and the last refill time. It adds tokens for the elapsed time at the refill rate, capped at the bucket capacity. If at least one token is left, it takes one and allows the request. It then saves the new state and sets a TTL so idle users do not use memory. It is a Lua script because Redis runs a script atomically. If two servers ran separate HGET and HSET commands, both could read 1 token and both could allow a request, which is a race. Each API server calls EVALSHA with the user's key, the capacity, the rate and the current time. Passing the time from the app risks clock skew between servers, so I would read time inside the script with redis.call('TIME'). If Redis is down, I fail open for most APIs and fail closed for sensitive ones such as login. A rejected request returns HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
keyPoints: Identifies the token bucket: refill by elapsed time, capacity cap, take one token per request
Atomic Lua execution prevents the read-modify-write race across servers
The TTL bounds memory for idle keys
Clock skew risk; use Redis TIME
Fail-open vs fail-closed choice, and a 429 response with Retry-After

subjective.question: In a distributed cache, one key (a celebrity profile) receives 500,000 reads per second and overloads the single node that owns it. How do you handle hot keys?
subjective.answer: First, I confirm the problem with per-key metrics, because consistent hashing sends one key to one node however many nodes we add. For read-heavy hot keys, I have three main tools. First, a small in-process L1 cache on each app server with a short TTL of a few seconds. This absorbs most reads and accepts slightly stale data. Second, key replication: store copies as profile:123#0 to profile:123#N spread across nodes, and have clients read a random suffix. Writes must update all copies, or the copies must expire quickly. Third, read replicas for the shard that owns the key. A CDN can also cache public profile data at the edge. For write-hot keys, such as a like counter, I split the counter into sub-counters and sum them on read, or batch increments. The trade-off is freshness and write cost against read capacity. I also detect hot keys automatically so I can apply these steps dynamically.
keyPoints: Consistent hashing alone cannot spread a single key
Local L1 cache with a short TTL, accepting slight staleness
Key replication with random suffixes; writes must update or expire the copies
Split counters for write-hot keys
Monitoring and automatic hot-key detection

subjective.question: Your Snowflake-style ID service suddenly produces duplicate IDs on one host after an NTP correction. Explain the cause and how you would make the generator safe.
subjective.answer: A Snowflake ID combines timestamp, worker ID and sequence. If NTP moves the clock backward, the host reuses milliseconds it has already issued. The same worker ID and sequence then produce IDs that already exist. A duplicate worker ID, for example two containers given the same ID, causes the same symptom, so I check that too. Fixes: the generator stores the last timestamp it used. If the current time is earlier, it either waits until the clock catches up, for small drifts, or refuses to issue IDs and raises an alert, for large drifts. Some designs keep using the last timestamp and borrow from the sequence bits. Configure NTP to slew the clock gradually rather than step it. Assign worker IDs from a coordinator such as ZooKeeper or a DynamoDB conditional write, with leases, so no two live processes share an ID. Finally, a unique constraint on the short-code table is a last line of defence.
keyPoints: Clock moving backward reuses timestamps, causing duplicates
Track the last timestamp; wait or fail when the clock regresses
NTP slewing instead of stepping
Unique worker ID assignment with leases
A database unique constraint as a safety net

subjective.question: Design online presence and 'last seen' for a WhatsApp-scale chat app with hundreds of millions of connected users. What trade-offs do you make?
subjective.answer: Each client holds a WebSocket to a gateway server. A heartbeat every 20 to 30 seconds refreshes a presence key in a sharded store such as Redis, for example presence:user = gateway_id, with a TTL of about two heartbeats. If heartbeats stop, the key expires and the user is offline. 'Last seen' is written when the key expires or the user disconnects. Pushing every status change to every contact causes huge fan-out. So I send updates only to contacts who have that chat open, or who subscribe while viewing it, and batch or debounce flapping on mobile networks. The trade-offs: presence is eventually consistent and can be wrong for up to the TTL window. A longer heartbeat interval saves battery and server load but makes status less fresh. Presence data is soft state, so losing a Redis shard is acceptable; it rebuilds from heartbeats. Privacy settings must be checked before showing last seen.
keyPoints: Heartbeats with TTL keys in a sharded in-memory store
Fan-out limited to active viewers or subscribers, with debouncing
Eventual consistency bounded by the TTL
Battery and load vs freshness trade-off
Presence is rebuildable soft state; privacy checks

subjective.question: A pastebin on AWS supports pastes that expire after 10 minutes, 1 day or never. Metadata is in DynamoDB and content is in S3. How do you implement expiry correctly and cheaply?
subjective.answer: I store an expires_at epoch attribute on each DynamoDB item and enable DynamoDB TTL on it. TTL deletes items for free, but deletion can be delayed, typically by up to a few days. So the read path must also check expires_at and return 404 if the time has passed. That check is what enforces correctness. For S3 content, I enable DynamoDB Streams and use a Lambda that deletes the S3 object when TTL removes the item. As a backup, I write objects under prefixes or tags by expiry class and add S3 Lifecycle rules, for example expire objects tagged ttl=1d after one day. Lifecycle rules work in whole days, so 10-minute pastes rely on the read check plus the stream cleanup. If a CDN caches pastes, its Cache-Control max-age must not exceed the remaining lifetime. 'Never' pastes get no TTL and can move to a cheaper storage class.
keyPoints: DynamoDB TTL is free but delayed; the read path must check expires_at
Streams plus Lambda to delete S3 objects
S3 Lifecycle rules as a backup, with day granularity
CDN max-age bounded by the remaining lifetime
Cost: cheaper storage classes for permanent pastes

subjective.question: Your web crawler's frontier keeps growing, and most new URLs come from a single site with URLs like /calendar?date=2031-01-01, /calendar?date=2031-01-02 and so on. Diagnose the problem and describe the fixes.
subjective.answer: This is a spider trap: a site that generates endless unique URLs, here a calendar, so the crawler never finishes the site and the frontier fills with low-value pages. Fixes, in layers: Normalise URLs by lowercasing the host, sorting query parameters and removing session IDs and tracking parameters. This collapses obvious duplicates. Set per-host and per-domain budgets, such as a maximum number of pages and a maximum URL depth. Limit URL length and the number of distinct values of one query parameter for the same path. Detect content duplicates with checksums or SimHash: if many URLs return near-identical content, lower that pattern's priority. Use the priority queue so low-value hosts do not starve others, and respect robots.txt, which often disallows such paths. Add manual blocklists and alerts when one host's share of the frontier spikes. The trade-off is that strict limits may miss some real pages, which is acceptable for most crawls.
keyPoints: Identifies the spider trap
URL normalisation
Per-host page and depth budgets, URL length and parameter limits
Content fingerprinting (checksum or SimHash) to detect near-duplicates
Prioritisation, robots.txt and monitoring host share

subjective.question: Your news feed uses fan-out on write into per-user Redis feed lists. How do you handle a user deleting a post, or a user unfollowing someone, without rewriting millions of feeds?
subjective.answer: I store only post IDs in feed lists, never post bodies. Post content lives in a post store and cache, and is hydrated at read time. For a delete, I mark the post as deleted in the post store and invalidate its cache entry. During hydration, deleted or hidden posts are filtered out, so they disappear from every feed at once without touching follower lists. An async background job can then remove the ID from feeds lazily, or the ID simply ages out because feeds are capped at a few hundred entries. For an unfollow, I filter at read time against the current follow graph, or run a low-priority async job that removes that author's IDs from the one affected feed, which is cheap. The same read-time filter handles blocks and privacy changes. The trade-off is a little extra read-time work and some dead IDs in the lists, in exchange for instant correctness and no write storms.
keyPoints: Feeds store post IDs; content is hydrated at read time
Soft delete plus filtering during hydration
Lazy cleanup, or let capped feeds age entries out
Unfollow handled by a read-time filter or a small async job
Trades read-time work for avoiding write storms

subjective.question: Case study: an Indian bank wants a URL shortener for SMS links. Requirements: 20 million links a day, links expire after 30 days, data must stay in India, 99.99% availability, no phishing abuse, and click analytics for marketing. Outline your design and the key decisions.
subjective.answer: First I would confirm the read-to-write ratio, the latency target and who can create links. At 20 million a day, writes average about 230 per second, so I would plan for roughly 700 at peak. I would place the system in two Indian AWS regions, Mumbai and Hyderabad. The API runs on API Gateway with ECS or Lambda. Data goes in DynamoDB global tables replicated between those two regions, with a TTL attribute for 30-day expiry. Each region gets pre-allocated code ranges, so codes never collide without cross-region coordination. To stop phishing, only internal bank services can create links, and targets must be on an allowlist of bank domains. Redirects return 302 so every click reaches us. Click events flow through Kinesis to S3 and are queried with Athena. Route 53 health checks fail over between the regions. Trade-off decision: I accept a few seconds of cross-region replication lag, which means AP behaviour, because a new link is used from the region that created it.
keyPoints: Clarify scale first and estimate about 230 writes/s average, about 700 at peak
Data residency: two Indian regions with DynamoDB global tables and TTL for expiry
Collision-free IDs with per-region ranges
Domain allowlist and authenticated creation to prevent phishing
302 redirects with an async analytics pipeline; state the AP decision

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: one Redis node that holds precomputed home feeds crashed. Within a minute, the posts database hit 100% CPU and feed latency went above 10 seconds for everyone. Explain why, and how you would recover and prevent it.
subjective.answer: The failed node's slice of feeds became cold all at once. Every request for those users missed the cache and rebuilt the feed from the posts database, which is an expensive query. Thousands of identical rebuilds ran in parallel. The database saturated, which also slowed users whose feeds were still cached. To recover, I would shed load first. I would rate-limit the rebuild path and use request coalescing, so only one rebuild per user runs at a time. Meanwhile I would serve a degraded feed, such as recent posts from a cached list of followed accounts, instead of a full ranked feed. A circuit breaker protects the database. To prevent it, I would run ElastiCache with replicas and Multi-AZ automatic failover, so a node loss promotes a warm replica. Consistent hashing means only one slice is affected. I would also rebuild lazily with jitter and keep a small, cheap fallback feed. Finally, I would load-test the 'cache node dies' scenario.
keyPoints: Cause: cold cache plus a thundering herd of expensive rebuilds
Immediate fixes: request coalescing, rate-limited rebuilds, circuit breaker, degraded feed
Prevention: replicas with automatic failover and consistent hashing
Rebuild lazily with jitter and test the failure on purpose

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this chat design proposal, and say how you would fix each one.

code.code:
chat_design:
  connections: WebSocket servers behind a load balancer
  routing: each WS server keeps user_id->socket in local memory;
           to deliver, broadcast every message to all WS servers
  storage: one MySQL table messages(id AUTO_INCREMENT, sender,
           receiver, body, created_at)
  ordering: ORDER BY created_at (client clock)
  offline: if receiver not connected, drop; client polls every 60s
  media: images sent as base64 inside body
  receipts: mark 'delivered' when the server writes to DB

subjective.answer: Broadcasting every message to all WebSocket servers costs O(servers) per message, which does not scale. I would keep a session registry, such as user_id to gateway server in Redis with a TTL heartbeat, and route each message only to the right server. A single MySQL table is a write bottleneck and a single point of failure. I would use a partitioned store such as Cassandra or DynamoDB, keyed by conversation_id with a sort key for time or sequence. Client clocks cannot order messages, so the server should assign a sequence number per conversation. Dropping messages for offline users loses data. I would store and forward instead: persist first, send a push notification, and let the client sync from its last sequence number on reconnect. Base64 media bloats messages and the database. Clients should upload to S3 with a pre-signed URL and send only the object key, with downloads served through a CDN. Finally, 'delivered' must mean the recipient device acknowledged the message. A server write only means 'sent'.
keyPoints: Session registry instead of broadcasting to all servers
Partitioned message store keyed by conversation
Server-assigned per-conversation sequence numbers
Store-and-forward with push and sync on reconnect for offline users
Media in object storage; delivered receipt comes from the device ACK

subjective.question: For finding nearby drivers, compare geohash, quadtree and a hexagonal grid such as H3. Which would you choose for a ride-hailing MVP in Indian cities, and why?
subjective.answer: Geohash encodes a location as a string prefix, so nearby points share prefixes. It is easy to store and shard, and Redis GEO uses a similar idea. Its weaknesses are edge effects and cells that change shape with latitude, so you must always search the neighbouring cells too. A quadtree splits busy areas into smaller cells, so it adapts well to dense cities and sparse highways. But it lives in memory, and rebalancing the tree with millions of updates every few seconds is costly to run. H3 hexagons have a uniform distance to all six neighbours. That makes 'k rings around me' searches and area aggregates such as surge pricing and demand heatmaps clean, but it adds a library dependency and conversion cost. For an MVP I would choose geohash or Redis GEO with a neighbour-cell search. It is simple, fast and well understood. Later I would move to H3 when surge pricing and supply-demand analytics need even cells. I would not pick a quadtree because the update rate is so high.
keyPoints: Geohash: simple prefix sharding but has boundary issues, so search neighbour cells
Quadtree: adapts to density but costly to update at high write rates
H3: uniform neighbours, good for surge pricing and aggregation
Make a decision: geohash or Redis GEO first, H3 later

subjective.question: List, in order, what happens from the moment a rider taps 'Book' until a driver is confirmed. Point out where failures can happen at each step.
subjective.answer: First, the app sends a booking request with the pickup location and an idempotency key. A retry after a network drop must not create two trips. Second, the trip service validates the request and stores a trip in the REQUESTED state. Third, the matching service queries the geo index for available drivers in the rider's cell and the neighbouring cells, widening the radius if there are too few. Fourth, it ranks candidates by ETA and other factors. Fifth, it offers the trip to the top driver. It uses an atomic conditional update to move that driver from AVAILABLE to OFFERED, with a short TTL, so two riders can never lock the same driver. Sixth, if the driver rejects or the TTL expires, it releases the driver and offers the trip to the next candidate. Seventh, on acceptance, the trip moves to ACCEPTED, and the rider is notified over WebSocket with a push notification as fallback. Failures to handle: a matching service crash, recovered by re-reading REQUESTED trips; stale locations, handled by ignoring old updated_at values; and no drivers, handled with a timeout message to the rider.
keyPoints: Idempotency key on the booking request
Trip state machine persisted before matching
Geo search over neighbouring cells, then ranking
Atomic conditional driver lock with TTL and fallback to the next driver
Notify the rider and recover from crashes using stored state

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a video platform's transcoding queue on Amazon SQS keeps growing after a viral event. Logs show the same video being transcoded by two or three workers at once, and compute cost has tripled. What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
subjective.answer: The most likely cause is that the SQS visibility timeout is shorter than the transcode time. For example, the timeout is 5 minutes but a long video takes 20. While the first worker is still working, the message becomes visible again and another worker picks it up. That duplicates work, slows the queue and wastes compute. To fix it, I would set the visibility timeout above the worst-case job time. Better, the worker should extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility as a heartbeat while it works. I would make the jobs idempotent: output keys depend on video_id and rendition, and a job state table uses a conditional write, so a duplicate exits early. I would split long videos into segments and transcode them in parallel, which shortens each job. I would set maxReceiveCount with a dead-letter queue for poison inputs, and autoscale workers on queue depth. I would also separate short and long videos into different queues so long jobs do not block quick ones.
keyPoints: Cause: visibility timeout shorter than processing time
Heartbeat with ChangeMessageVisibility or a longer timeout
Idempotent jobs with deterministic output keys
Chunked parallel transcoding, a DLQ and autoscaling on queue depth

subjective.question: This token bucket runs inside each of 20 API servers behind a round-robin load balancer. Find the mistakes and propose a correct design.

code.code:
buckets = {}  # user_id -> (tokens, last_ts)
RATE = 100 / 60   # tokens per second
CAP = 100

def allow(user_id):
    now = time.time()
    tokens, last = buckets.get(user_id, (CAP, now))
    tokens = min(CAP, tokens + (now - last) * RATE)
    if tokens >= 1:
        buckets[user_id] = (tokens - 1, now)
        return True
    buckets[user_id] = (tokens, now)
    return False

subjective.answer: The state lives in each process. With 20 servers and round robin, a user effectively gets about 20 times the limit, and the count is wrong on every server. The state is lost when a server restarts or scales. The dictionary grows without limit because nothing is evicted. The read-modify-write is not thread-safe, so concurrent requests can both spend the same token. time.time() can jump when the clock changes, so a monotonic or shared time source is safer. A correct design keeps one bucket per user in Redis, such as ElastiCache with replicas. A Lua script reads, refills and deducts atomically, using Redis TIME as the single clock, and the key has a TTL so idle users expire. I would shard users across the cluster and decide what happens when Redis fails. Usually I would fail open with a conservative local limit. Rejected requests get HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.
keyPoints: Per-process state makes the limit about N times too high
State is lost on restart, and memory grows without eviction
Race condition and wall-clock jumps
Shared Redis with an atomic Lua script, a single clock and key TTL
Fail-open policy and 429 with Retry-After

subjective.question: For the queue layer of a notification system that sends push, SMS and email, compare Amazon SQS (with SNS) and Kafka (for example Amazon MSK). Which would you pick, and when would you change your mind?
subjective.answer: SQS is fully managed and acknowledges each message. Visibility timeouts, dead-letter queues and autoscaling work out of the box, and you do not plan for partitions. That fits notifications well: each job is independent, a failed message goes to the DLQ, and SNS fan-out can feed one queue per channel and priority. Its limits are that you cannot replay old messages once they are consumed, and standard queues give no strict ordering. Kafka keeps an ordered, replayable log with very high throughput. Many consumer groups, such as senders, analytics and audit, can read the same events independently. But it needs partition planning and lag monitoring. A slow or poison message blocks its partition, so retries and DLQs must be built by hand. I would choose SNS plus SQS, with separate queues per channel and per priority. OTPs go in a high-priority queue so marketing blasts cannot delay them. I would add Kafka if we needed event replay, a shared event log for many teams, or strict per-user ordering at very high volume.
keyPoints: SQS: managed, per-message ack, DLQ and visibility timeout built in
Kafka: replayable ordered log and multiple consumer groups, but more operations work
Per-channel and per-priority queues so OTPs beat marketing
Make a decision and state when to switch

subjective.question: Case study: design search autocomplete for an Indian e-commerce app. Users type in English, Hindi (Devanagari) and Hinglish. The target is p99 under 50 ms at sale-day peaks. Suggestions must be personalised a little, and offensive terms must never appear.
subjective.answer: First I would clarify how many top suggestions to show, how fresh they must be, and the peak QPS. Offline, a pipeline aggregates search logs and conversion signals. It normalises text with Unicode NFC normalisation and lowercasing, and transliterates Hinglish and Devanagari to a shared phonetic key, so 'joote' and 'जूते' map together. It then builds top-k lists per prefix and applies a blocklist and moderation step before anything is published. Serving uses an in-memory prefix map or trie, sharded by prefix and replicated across availability zones. Results for very short prefixes are cached at the CDN or in an edge cache because they are the hottest. The client debounces keystrokes and caches recent responses. For personalisation, the client blends its own recent searches with the global list, which avoids a per-user server index. A streaming layer adds trending queries during sales. Trade-off decision: I accept suggestions that are minutes old, because speed matters more than perfect freshness. The blocklist is enforced at both build time and serve time.
keyPoints: Normalisation and transliteration so scripts map to one key
Offline top-k per prefix with a blocklist at build and serve time
Sharded, replicated in-memory serving with an edge cache for short prefixes
Client debounce and lightweight client-side personalisation
Streaming layer for trends; accept minutes of staleness

subjective.question: Troubleshooting: a key-value store uses N=3, W=2, R=2 and last-write-wins conflict resolution based on each node's wall-clock timestamp. A user updated their profile twice, a second apart, but the store kept the first update. Quorums overlap, so how did this happen, and what would you change?
subjective.answer: Quorum overlap only ensures a read sees the version that the versioning scheme says is newest. It does not ensure that version is the real latest. Here the first write was stamped by a node whose clock ran ahead, so its timestamp was higher than the second write's. Last-write-wins then threw away the correct, later update without any warning. Clock skew of hundreds of milliseconds is normal in a cluster. There are three ways to fix it. One is version vectors: they detect concurrent writes and keep both as siblings for the application or a merge rule to resolve. Another is conditional writes with a per-key version number, routed through a leader for each key, so an update succeeds only if it builds on the version it read. Hybrid logical clocks reduce skew damage but do not remove it. For counters and sets, CRDTs merge safely. For profiles, I would choose leader-based compare-and-set, because losing a user's edit without notice is not acceptable.
keyPoints: Quorum guarantees overlap, not correct ordering
LWW with skewed wall clocks silently drops later writes
Version vectors with siblings, or CAS with a per-key leader
CRDTs for mergeable data; choose CAS for profiles

subjective.question: Spot the mistakes in this web crawler configuration, and give a corrected setting for each.

code.code:
crawler:
  workers: 2000
  per_host_concurrency: 200
  per_host_delay_ms: 0
  obey_robots_txt: false
  max_depth: unlimited
  max_urls_per_host: unlimited
  dedupe: exact_url_string
  retry: {max_attempts: 10, backoff: none}
  store_pages_in: postgres.pages.html_column
  user_agent: "Mozilla/5.0"

subjective.answer: 200 parallel requests to one host with no delay is effectively an attack, so expect bans. I would allow one or two connections per host, set a per-host delay, and honour Crawl-delay where present. Ignoring robots.txt is both impolite and a legal risk. I would fetch it, cache it per host and always obey it. Unlimited depth and unlimited URLs per host let spider traps, such as endless calendars, consume the frontier. I would set depth and per-host budgets. Deduping on the exact URL string misses variants. I would normalise URLs by lowercasing the host, stripping tracking parameters and sorting the query string, and also dedupe pages by content fingerprint, for example SimHash. Ten retries with no backoff hammer servers that are already failing. I would use about three attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, and back off for the whole host when it returns 429 or 503. Storing HTML in Postgres bloats the database. Page bodies belong in S3, with only metadata in the database. Finally, a fake browser user agent hides who we are. I would use an honest bot name with a contact URL.
keyPoints: Per-host politeness: low concurrency and a delay
Obey robots.txt and cache it per host
Depth and per-host budgets against spider traps
URL normalisation plus content fingerprint dedupe
Backoff with jitter, blobs in object storage, an honest user agent

subjective.question: For sending images and videos in a chat app, which is better: uploading through the chat servers, or having clients upload directly to Amazon S3 with pre-signed URLs? Explain your choice.
subjective.answer: Uploading through the chat servers keeps all access control in one place. But every megabyte passes through stateful WebSocket servers that are built for small messages. They become bandwidth and memory bottlenecks, and one large upload can slow message delivery for thousands of users on the same server. Direct upload with a pre-signed URL moves the heavy traffic straight to S3, which scales on its own. The chat server only issues a short-lived URL scoped to one object key, with limits on content type and size through a pre-signed POST policy. The message then carries only the object key and some metadata. I would choose pre-signed uploads. Downloads go through CloudFront with signed URLs or cookies. A background job creates thumbnails and scans the files. S3 lifecycle rules move old media to cheaper storage classes. For end-to-end encryption, the client encrypts the file before upload and sends the key inside the encrypted message, so the server stores only ciphertext.
keyPoints: Proxying media through chat servers creates bandwidth and latency bottlenecks
Pre-signed URLs are short-lived, scoped and size-limited
Messages carry only the object key; CDN for downloads
Async thumbnails, scanning and lifecycle rules; client-side encryption for E2E

subjective.question: Interviewers often ask, 'What happens when things break?' For your URL shortener, walk through four failures: the cache cluster dies, one database shard dies, the ID generation service dies, and a whole region goes down.
subjective.answer: Cache cluster dies: redirects fall back to the database. To stop a stampede, I use replicas with automatic failover, request coalescing, and rate limits on the miss path. A local in-process LRU cache for the hottest codes absorbs part of the load. One shard dies: each shard has replicas, and a replica is promoted, as with Multi-AZ failover or DynamoDB's built-in replication. Only keys on that shard see a short error spike, and clients retry with backoff. ID service dies: each app server already holds a pre-allocated range of IDs. It can keep creating codes until the range runs out, so a short outage does not stop writes. Region goes down: Route 53 health checks fail over to a second region that holds replicated data. Redirects keep working. New writes can either pause or use that region's own ID ranges. My decision is to keep redirects available and accept a short write pause, because reads are about 90% of traffic.
keyPoints: Cache loss: failover replicas, coalescing, local LRU, a protected miss path
Shard loss: replica promotion and client retries with backoff
ID service loss: pre-allocated ranges keep writes going
Region loss: DNS failover; prefer read availability over writes

steps.overview: This final step turns everything you learned into two outcomes: a repeatable 4-step interview framework (clarify, estimate, high-level design, deep dive) and a mapping from generic patterns to the AWS services that SAA-C03 tests. You will also learn the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework, which shape how scenario questions are written and how interviewers judge trade-offs.
objectives: Run a 45-minute system design interview using the clarify, estimate, high-level design and deep dive framework inside the time box.
Explain trade-offs out loud by naming the options, the deciding requirement and the cost of the choice.
Map load balancing, scaling, caching, relational storage, NoSQL storage and queueing patterns to ELB, Auto Scaling, ElastiCache, RDS, DynamoDB and SQS.
Apply the six Well-Architected pillars to eliminate wrong answers in SAA-C03 scenario questions.
Score above 80% on a full-length SAA-C03 practice exam and review every wrong answer by domain.

concepts.explanation: Spend about 5 minutes asking about users, core features, read/write ratio, latency targets, consistency needs and availability goals. Write down functional requirements (what it does) and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, durability). Agree on what is out of scope so you do not design features nobody asked for.

Convert daily users into requests per second, storage per year and bandwidth. Round aggressively: 1 day is about 100,000 seconds, and peak is often 2–3x average. The numbers decide whether you need sharding, caching or a queue, so say that link out loud.

Draw the main boxes: client, CDN, load balancer, stateless app tier, cache, database, queue and workers. Walk one read path and one write path end to end. Keep it simple first; an interviewer wants a working design before an optimised one.

Pick the one or two hardest parts, such as the data model, hot keys, fan-out or failure handling, and go deep. Discuss bottlenecks, single points of failure, consistency and monitoring. Let the interviewer steer you if they show interest in a component.

Use a simple pattern: 'Option A gives X, option B gives Y; because our requirement is Z, I choose A, and the cost is W.' Typical pairs are SQL vs NoSQL, strong vs eventual consistency, push vs pull fan-out and cache-aside vs write-through. Saying the cost of your choice shows seniority more than the choice itself.

Load balancer maps to Elastic Load Balancing (ALB for HTTP/HTTPS at layer 7, NLB for TCP/UDP at layer 4 with static IPs). Horizontal scaling maps to EC2 Auto Scaling groups across multiple AZs. Cache maps to ElastiCache (Redis OSS or Valkey for rich data types and replication, Memcached for simple multi-threaded caching), relational data to RDS or Aurora, key-value at massive scale to DynamoDB, and decoupling to SQS.

Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ for automatic failover; it is for availability, not read scaling. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be promoted manually. Exam rule: 'high availability' points to Multi-AZ, while 'read-heavy workload' points to read replicas or a cache.

Standard queues give at-least-once delivery, best-effort ordering and very high throughput. FIFO queues give strict ordering and exactly-once processing, with lower throughput limits. Use SQS to absorb spikes and decouple producers from consumers, and scale the workers on queue depth.

It has six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. SAA-C03 questions often hide one pillar as the deciding factor, for example 'most cost-effective' or 'least operational overhead'. In interviews, use the pillars as a final checklist for your design.

keyFacts: SAA-C03: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored), 130 minutes, pass mark 720 on a 100–1000 scale, USD 150.
SAA-C03 domain weights: Design Secure Architectures 30%, Design Resilient Architectures 26%, Design High-Performing Architectures 24%, Design Cost-Optimized Architectures 20%.
Well-Architected has six pillars; Sustainability was added in 2021 as the sixth.
A 45-minute interview time box: about 5 min clarify, 5 min estimate, 15 min high-level design, 15–20 min deep dive and wrap-up.
Estimation shortcuts: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s (use 100,000); 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 requests/second average.
SQS visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds (max 12 hours); message retention defaults to 4 days (max 14 days).
DynamoDB maximum item size is 400 KB; for large objects, store them in S3 and keep a pointer in DynamoDB.
ALB = layer 7 with path- and host-based routing; NLB = layer 4, ultra-low latency, static/Elastic IP per AZ.
Keywords in a question decide the answer: 'least operational overhead' points to managed or serverless services, and 'decouple' points to SQS/SNS.

example.caption: Worked estimate and AWS mapping for a URL shortener (spoken in Step 2 and Step 3)
example.code:
Clarify: 100M new URLs/month, read:write = 100:1, p99 redirect < 50 ms, 5-year retention

Estimate:
  Writes: 100M / (30 x 100,000 s) ~= 35 writes/s (peak ~100/s)
  Reads:  35 x 100 ~= 3,500 reads/s (peak ~10,000/s)
  Storage: 100M x 12 months x 5 yrs = 6B rows x ~500 B ~= 3 TB
  Decision: read-heavy, simple key lookup -> cache + key-value store

High-level design (AWS):
  Route 53 -> CloudFront -> ALB -> EC2 Auto Scaling group (multi-AZ, stateless)
  Read path: app -> ElastiCache (cache-aside, TTL 24h) -> DynamoDB on miss
  Write path: app -> DynamoDB (partition key = short_code)
  Analytics: app -> SQS -> worker fleet -> S3 (click logs)

Trade-off said out loud:
  'DynamoDB over RDS because access is a single-key lookup at 10k reads/s
   and 3 TB grows steadily; I give up ad-hoc SQL joins, which we do not need.'

Well-Architected check:
  Reliability: multi-AZ ASG, DynamoDB replicated across AZs
  Cost: on-demand DynamoDB first, then provisioned capacity once traffic is known
  Security: HTTPS on ALB, IAM roles for EC2, no secrets in code

pitfalls: Jumping to the diagram before clarifying requirements; interviewers mark this down even if the design is good.
Doing estimates and then never using them; every number should drive a decision such as cache, shard or queue.
Choosing RDS Multi-AZ to scale reads; the standby does not serve reads, so use read replicas or ElastiCache.
Ignoring qualifier words like 'most cost-effective', 'least operational overhead' or 'minimal code change'; on the exam, several options often work, but only one matches the qualifier.
Choosing SQS FIFO by default; pick it only when strict ordering or exactly-once processing is required, because Standard scales further.
Spending the whole deep dive on one component and running out of time; watch the clock and summarise at the end.

files.code:
# shortlink-mock-design (Step 9: Interview framework)

Practise one system design question end to end: "Design a URL shortener".

## 1. Mock interview (do this twice, with a friend)
- `python3 interview/mock_interview.py` runs a 45-minute time box:
  clarify 5, estimate 5, high-level design 15, deep dive 15, wrap-up 5.
- Your friend reads the prompts aloud. You talk through every trade-off.
